PixelPlane<Rgba8> plane = image.Frames[0].Plane; if (plane.TryGetContiguous(out Span<Rgba8> all)) { all.Fill(Rgba8.White); // one Span over every pixel when the rows are stored back to back } else { for (int y = 0; y < plane.Height; y++) { plane.Row(y).Fill(Rgba8.White); } } RasterOps records each step of a chain; built-in steps and your own mix freely. // RasterOps records steps; Apply runs them in one pass where it can, in place when the size stays. using Raster photo = Raster.Load("egret.png"); photo.Apply(ops => ops .AutoOrient() .Cover(400, 300, Anchor.Center) .Saturation(1.1f) .Sharpen(1, 0.6f)); /// <summary>Black or white per pixel: ForEachBand gives each worker a band of rows from start to end.</summary> private sealed class Threshold(float level) : IRasterOperation { public Size OutputSize(Size input) => input; public void Run<TPixel>(OperationInput<TPixel> input) where TPixel : unmanaged, IPixelType<TPixel> { RowBandAction band = (start, end) => { for (int y = start; y < end; y++) { Span<TPixel> source = input.Source.Row(y), destination = input.Destination.Row(y); for (int x = 0; x < source.Length; x++) { Vector4 v = source[x].ToScaled(); float on = ((0.2126f * v.X) + (0.7152f * v.Y) + (0.0722f * v.Z)) >= level ? 1 : 0; destination[x] = TPixel.FromScaled(new Vector4(on, on, on, v.W)); } } }; input.ForEachBand(band); } } Run it samples/Extending is a console app that does what this guide shows on the bundled images: dotnet run --project samples/Extending writes its results to ./output.

articles/guides/filters.html.title: Filters | Egami
articles/guides/filters.html.summary: Filters using Raster soft = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Blur(3), Ct); // Gaussian, sigma in pixels using Raster boxed = photo.Derive(ops => ops.BoxBlur(4), Ct); // fast, radius in pixels using Raster crisp = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Sharpen(0.8f, 1.5f), Ct); // unsharp mask: amount, sigma // Any kernel: here a 3 × 3 emboss, with edges clamped and alpha left alone. ConvolutionKernel emboss = new(3, 3, [-2, -1, 0, -1, 1, 1, 0, 1, 2]); using Raster embossed = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Convolve(emboss, EdgeMode.Clamp, preserveAlpha: true), Ct); Operation Does Blur(sigma, colorSpace) Gaussian blur, separable; exact up to sigma 100, three box passes above Blur(sigma, colorSpace, BlurMethod.Fast) Gaussian blur in constant time per pixel at any sigma, for shadows, glows and large blurs BoxBlur(radius) Mean of a square, in constant time per pixel whatever the radius Sharpen(amount, sigma) Unsharp mask: adds amount times the difference from a Gaussian blur Convolve(kernel, edge, preserveAlpha) Any ConvolutionKernel, separable ones in two passes Median(radius, includeAlpha) The median of each channel over a square: removes salt-and-pepper noise, keeps edges LensBlur(radius, options) An out-of-focus lens: points become discs or polygons BilateralBlur(spatialSigma, rangeSigma) Smooths flat areas, keeps edges MotionBlur(radius, sigma, angle) A streak in one direction, as ImageMagick's -motion-blur RotationalBlur(degrees, center) A spin around a point, as ImageMagick's -rotational-blur ZoomBlur(amount, center) Streaks along rays from a point AddNoise(kind, amount, monochrome, seed) ImageMagick's six noise kinds, the same for a seed at any thread count Despeckle() Crimmins' speckle removal, as ImageMagick's -despeckle Large blurs Blur(sigma) computes the exact Gaussian, so its cost grows with sigma. BlurMethod.Fast runs three box passes per axis whose widths and fractional end weights give exactly the Gaussian's variance (Gwosdek et al., 2011): it costs the same at sigma 5 or 500, about six times less than the exact blur at sigma 20, and stays within 50 dB PSNR of it from sigma 3 up. // A large, soft background blur: Fast costs the same at any sigma and is within 50 dB of the exact Gaussian from sigma 3. using Raster soft = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Blur(40, ColorSpace.Linear, BlurMethod.Fast), Ct); Median and despeckle Median works on the stored values, so 8 and 16-bit results are exactly ImageMagick's -statistic Median. Its cost per pixel does not grow with the radius. Despeckle is gentler: it nudges values a level at a time toward their neighbours and leaves edges alone, exactly as ImageMagick's -despeckle. // Salt-and-pepper noise disappears and edges stay sharp; radius 2 is a 5 × 5 window. photo.Apply(ops => ops.Median(2), Ct); // Clean a scan: specks shrink, edges and text stay. Median(1) is the stronger alternative. scan.Apply(ops => ops.Despeckle(), Ct); Lens and bilateral blur LensBlur convolves with an aperture: a disc, or a polygon of 5 to 12 blades turned by Rotation. It works in linear light, since a lens adds light, and HighlightGain brightens light above HighlightThreshold before the blur, so small lights bloom into bright discs. It runs by FFT on tiles, so its cost does not grow with the radius. // Blur the background like a wide-open lens with a six-blade aperture: bright points become hexagons. LensBlurOptions lens = new() { Blades = 6, Rotation = 15, HighlightGain = 4, HighlightThreshold = 0.8f }; photo.Apply(ops => ops.Within(new Rect(0, 0, photo.Width, photo.Height / 3), o => o.LensBlur(12, lens)), Ct); BilateralBlur weighs each neighbour by its distance and by how different its color is, so noise flattens and edges stay. The color difference is the root-mean-square difference of red, green and blue on 0..1; on gray images the sigmas mean what ImageMagick's -bilateral-blur means, with its intensity sigma 255 times rangeSigma. // Smooth skin or sky while keeping edges: neighbours count less the more their color differs (0.1 on the 0..1 scale). using Raster smooth = photo.Derive(ops => ops.BilateralBlur(spatialSigma: 4, rangeSigma: 0.1f), Ct); Directional blurs MotionBlur takes ImageMagick's parameters: 2⌈radius⌉ + 1 samples along angle (clockwise, y down), weighted by a Gaussian of sigma. Egami reads between pixels bilinearly where ImageMagick rounds to the nearest pixel, so diagonal streaks are smoother. RotationalBlur and ZoomBlur take about one sample per pixel of path; their center is in pixels, with pixel centers at +0.5. using Raster moving = photo.Derive(ops => ops.MotionBlur(radius: 12, sigma: 4, angle: 15), Ct); // a streak toward 15° using Raster spinning = photo.Derive(ops => ops.RotationalBlur(8), Ct); // 8° around the center using Raster zooming = photo.Derive(ops => ops.ZoomBlur(0.2f, new System.Numerics.Vector2(320, 200)), Ct); Noise AddNoise adds ImageMagick's +noise kinds to red, green and blue, never alpha, with amount as ImageMagick's -attenuate. Each value's noise is a hash of the seed, frame and position, so the same seed gives the same pixels at any thread count, and inside Within an area gets the noise the whole image would get there. // Film grain: gray Gaussian noise at a third of ImageMagick's default strength; the same seed gives the same grain. photo.Apply(ops => ops.AddNoise(NoiseKind.Gaussian, 0.3f, monochrome: true, seed: 42), Ct); Edges EdgeMode says what a kernel sees past the border: Clamp repeats the edge pixel (the default), Mirror reflects the image, Wrap tiles it, and Transparent treats it as transparent black. The filters above repeat the edge pixel, as ImageMagick's default virtual pixel does. Alpha Blurs work on premultiplied values internally, so transparent pixels do not bleed their color into opaque ones. preserveAlpha: true keeps the alpha channel as it was, for effects that should only change color. Median and Despeckle keep alpha unless asked; AddNoise never touches it. Run it samples/Filters is a console app that does what this guide shows on the bundled images: dotnet run --project samples/Filters writes its results to ./output.

articles/guides/formats.html.title: Formats | Egami
articles/guides/formats.html.summary: Formats Egami reads and writes PNG, APNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, BMP, TGA, QOI and the Netpbm formats (PBM, PGM, PPM, PAM and the PFM float map), TIFF, Radiance .hdr, OpenEXR, JPEG XL, and Windows icons and cursors, and reads AVIF, JBIG2, raw CCITT fax data, JPEG 2000 and Photoshop's PSD and PSB. SVG and Windows metafiles (WMF, EMF) load through the separate Egami.Svg and Egami.Metafiles packages. Every reader checks sizes against the safety limits before it allocates, and every reader has been fuzzed. At a glance Format Reads Writes Natural pixel type PNG Every color type and bit depth, interlaced, transparency, text, EXIF, XMP, ICC Every color type and bit depth, adaptive filtering, built palettes, Adam7 interlacing, compression on several cores The file's own: Gray8, Gray16, GrayAlpha8, Rgb8, Rgba8 or Rgba16 APNG Every PNG color type and depth, every disposal and blend Any raster with more than one frame, changed rectangles only Rgba8, or Rgba16 for 16-bit JPEG Baseline, extended and progressive, Huffman or arithmetic, 8 and 12-bit, lossless at 2 to 16 bits, any subsampling, gray, CMYK, YCCK, scaled decode, EXIF, XMP, ICC Baseline or progressive, 8 or 12-bit, quality 1 to 100, 4:4:4, 4:2:2, 4:2:0, gray, CMYK or YCCK, optimized Huffman tables Gray8 or Rgb8; Gray16, Rgb16 or Cmyk16 above 8 bits GIF 87a and 89a, every disposal, interlaced, transparency, loop count, comments, XMP, ICC 89a, exact or quantized palettes, global or per frame, dithering, frame optimization Rgba8 WebP Lossless (VP8L) with every transform; lossy (VP8) with alpha, as RGB or as YUV planes; ICC, EXIF, XMP; see the WebP guide Lossless at effort 0 to 6, exact transparent colors; ICC, EXIF with resolution, XMP Rgb8, or Rgba8 with alpha BMP Core, info, V2 to V5 and OS/2 2.x headers; 1 to 32 bits; RLE4, RLE8, RLE24; bit fields; embedded PNG and JPEG; V5 ICC 24-bit, 32-bit with alpha, 1, 2, 4 or 8-bit palettes; resolution and ICC Bgr8, or Bgra8 with alpha TGA Color-mapped, true-color and gray, raw and RLE, 8 to 32 bits, all origins, TGA 2.0 footer and extension area 8-bit gray, 24 and 32-bit, 8-bit palette, raw or RLE, TGA 2.0 footer Bgr8, Bgra8, Gray8 or GrayAlpha8 QOI The whole format, 3 or 4 channels, both colorspaces 3 or 4 channels, byte-identical to the reference encoder Rgb8 or Rgba8 TIFF Every page, strips and tiles, chunky and planar, classic and BigTIFF; None, LZW, Deflate, PackBits, CCITT G3 and G4, JPEG, old-style JPEG, ThunderScan, SGILog, WebP, JPEG XL; gray, palette, RGB, CMYK, YCbCr, Lab and LogLuv at 1 to 64 bits; see the TIFF guide Every pixel type at its own depth, strips or tiles, classic or BigTIFF; None, LZW, Deflate, PackBits, CCITT G3 and G4, JPEG, WebP The page's own: Gray8, Gray16, Rgb8, Rgb16, Cmyk8, Cmyk16, float types and more CCITT Raw Group 3 and Group 4 data (T.4, T.6) with PDF's eight CCITTFaxDecode parameters, byte-aligned rows included; see the CCITT guide No Gray8, black 0 and white 255 JBIG2 Every T.88 region and dictionary but the colour extension; standalone files (sequential and random-access, many pages) and the embedded form a PDF holds, with its globals; see the JBIG2 guide No Gray8, black 0 and white 255 JPEG 2000 All of Part 1 (T.800): every progression order, code-block style, tiling and precinct size, reversible and irreversible; JP2 and JPX boxes, palettes, channel definitions, sYCC, CIELab, ICC; layer records and resources as metadata; see the PSD guide No By mode and depth: Gray8, Rgb8, Rgba8, Cmyk8, their 16-bit forms, float types Radiance RGBE and XYZE, every scan order, flat, old repeat-pixel and per-channel run-length scanlines; linear JPEG XL Every still, lossless Modular and lossy VarDCT or Modular, at 1 to 31 bits and float, with alpha, CMYK, extra channels, animations and layers, previews, PQ and HLG, gain maps, and recompressed JPEGs (given back byte for byte); see the JPEG XL guide Lossless in the raster's own precision, or lossy VarDCT in XYB, at cjxl's effort and quality scales; JPEGs recompressed losslessly By bit depth: Rgb8, Rgba8, Gray8, their 16-bit forms, RgbaF16 for 16-bit float, RgbF32, RgbaF32 or GrayF32 beyond AVIF Still images: AV1 intra frames with every coding tool, equal to dav1d's decode and converted to RGB as libavif does; alpha, grids, overlays, clean aperture, orientation, ICC, CICP, HDR, gain maps, every item, and sequences of key frames; see the AVIF guide No By bit depth: Rgb8 or Rgba8 for 8-bit files, Rgb16 or Rgba16 for 10 and 12 bits, Gray8 or Gray16 (with alpha, GrayAlpha8 or GrayAlpha16) for monochrome PNM P1 to P6 plain and binary, maxval 1 to 65,535, P7 PAM with alpha, PF and Pf float maps P1 to P7, plain or binary; PF and Pf Gray8, Gray16, GrayAlpha8, Rgb8, Rgba8 or Rgba16; RgbF32 or GrayF32 for PFM Raster.Load returns the natural type; Raster.Load<TPixel> decodes straight into the type you ask for, converting row by row. using Raster image = Raster.Load("duck.png"); switch (image) { case Raster<Rgb8> rgb: Console.WriteLine($"8-bit color, {rgb.Width} × {rgb.Height}"); break; case Raster<Rgba8> rgba: Console.WriteLine($"8-bit color with alpha, {rgba.Width} × {rgba.Height}"); break; default: Console.WriteLine($"{image.Layout.ChannelOrder}, {image.Layout.ChannelType}"); break; } Detection Loading never trusts the file extension: the format comes from the first bytes, in the order PNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, BMP, QOI, PNM, TIFF, JBIG2, JPEG 2000, ICO, CUR, PSD, Radiance, OpenEXR, JPEG XL (FF 0A or its signature box), AVIF (an ftyp box with the avif or avis brand), then TGA. TGA has no signature, so it is matched only when its whole 18-byte header is consistent. No file of another format in Egami's test corpora is taken for TGA, and neither is any of a million random headers. When you know the format, register only that one: // TGA has no signature, so it is detected last. When you know a file is TGA, register only that format. EgamiContext tgaOnly = EgamiContext.Default with { Formats = [TgaFormat.Info] }; using Raster image = Raster.Load("duck.tga", tgaOnly); Data without a signature of its own, such as the JBIG2 or CCITT stream of a PDF image, loads with its format named, which skips detection. Load, LoadAll, Probe and RasterDecoder.Open all take the format this way; naming the wrong one throws CorruptDataException, as damaged data of that format would. // Data without a signature of its own (a TGA here; a JBIG2 stream from a PDF) loads with its format named, // which skips detection. Probe, LoadAll and RasterDecoder.Open take the format the same way. using Raster image = Raster.Load(data, TgaFormat.Info); RasterInfo info = Raster.Probe(data, TgaFormat.Info); Saving to a path picks the writer from the extension; an animated raster saved as .png writes an APNG. Saving to a stream takes the format's Info. Several images in one file Frames are animation and share one size. A TIFF's pages are separate images, each with its own size and pixel type, so they come as a RasterList from Raster.LoadAll, which owns them; RasterInfo.ImageCount says how many there are. Every other format gives its one image, so LoadAll works on any file. Raster.SaveAll writes several rasters to a format that holds several, and one raster to any format. // Every page at its own size and pixel type. The list owns the rasters. using RasterList pages = Raster.LoadAll("scan.tif"); foreach (Raster page in pages) { Console.WriteLine($"{page.Width} × {page.Height}"); } // Keep one page after the list is gone. using Raster first = pages.Detach(0); PNG using FileStream output = File.Create("duck-small.png"); image.Save(output, PngFormat.Info, new PngWriterOptions { Reduce = true, // the smallest exact form: no alpha if all opaque, gray or a palette when nothing is lost CompressionLevel = 9, // 0 (fastest) to 9 (smallest); 5 by default }); Option Default Does ColorType, BitDepth The pixel type's own Force a layout, such as PngColorType.Palette Reduce false Scan the image and write the smallest exact form Palette 256 colors, Floyd–Steinberg How a palette is built when ColorType is Palette and the image has more colors CompressionLevel 5 zlib level, 0 to 9 Filter Adaptive Row filter, or one fixed filter FirstFrameOnly false Write a still PNG from an animation Interlace false Write Adam7, so a viewer can show a coarse image early; files are usually larger ParallelCompression false Compress images with more than 4 MiB of image data on several cores Interlace is never taken from the source: an interlaced PNG is written plain unless you set it. With ParallelCompression, the image data is cut into fixed bands of 1 MiB that compress on up to EgamiContext.MaxParallelism threads. The file is the same on any machine and at any thread count, and in Egami's tests it was 0.1% to 0.3% larger; a 24-megapixel photo saved 8 times as fast on 12 cores. Smaller images are written exactly as with the option off. image.Save("duck-large.png", new PngWriterOptions { ParallelCompression = true, // big images compress on several cores; the same file at any thread count Interlace = true, // Adam7: a coarse image shows before the whole file has arrived }); Kept for round trips in PngDetails: gamma, chromaticities, sRGB intent, cICP, the ICC profile name, and every chunk Egami does not read itself. BMP // Auto (the default): 24-bit when every pixel is opaque, 32-bit with alpha otherwise. image.Save("duck.bmp"); // A 16-color palette, built from the image and dithered. image.Save("duck-16.bmp", new BmpWriterOptions { PixelFormat = BmpPixelFormat.Indexed4 }); A plain 32-bit BMP's fourth byte is used as alpha unless it is 0 in every pixel, in which case the image loads opaque; an alpha mask in the header is always used. Pixels that an RLE delta skips are black. BmpPixelFormat.Indexed2 writes Windows CE 2-bit files, which many desktop readers cannot open, so Auto never picks it. Resolution is written in pixels per meter, and an ICC profile switches the header to V5 with the profile embedded. TGA // Run-length encoded by default, bottom-left origin, with a TGA 2.0 footer that states the alpha type. image.Save("duck.tga"); image.Save("duck-raw.tga", new TgaWriterOptions { Rle = false }); The descriptor's attribute bits say whether the extra bits are alpha, and a TGA 2.0 alpha type of "none" overrides them; premultiplied alpha is divided out on load. The extension area's author and comments become Author and Comment text entries, and the writer stores them back. TgaPixelFormat.Bgr24 drops alpha rather than blending it onto a background. QOI // 3 channels when every pixel is opaque, 4 otherwise. The bytes match the reference encoder's. image.Save("duck.qoi"); image.Save("duck-rgba.qoi", new QoiWriterOptions { IncludeAlpha = true }); QOI's colorspace byte maps to RasterMetadata.ColorSpace (sRGB or linear) and back. PNM // Auto: P5 (PGM) for gray, P6 (PPM) for color, P7 (PAM) when the pixel type has alpha. image.Save("duck.ppm"); // The plain-text forms, for tools that read them; lines are at most 70 characters. image.Save("duck-plain.ppm", new PnmWriterOptions { PlainText = true }); // A 1-bit bitmap, thresholded at 50% gray. image.Save("duck.pbm", new PnmWriterOptions { Kind = PnmKind.Bitmap }); Maxvals other than 255 and 65,535 are scaled exactly, as round(v × 255 / maxval). A PAM with an unknown tuple type is read by its depth, with a warning. A stream with several images reads the first and warns. # comments become Comment text entries and are written back. Saving to a .pbm, .pgm, .ppm, .pam or .pfm path writes that variant unless PnmWriterOptions.Kind names one; .pnm chooses from the pixel type. PFM float maps load as RgbF32 (PF) or GrayF32 (Pf), marked as linear light, with their scale and byte order in PnmDetails; values outside 0..1 are kept. Writing uses PFM for float types without alpha, or when PnmKind.FloatMap is asked for: little-endian, scale −1, as Netpbm and ImageMagick write it. What each writer drops Writers never change the raster. When a format cannot hold something, it is left out: Alpha: JPEG (unless JpegWriterOptions.Background blends it onto a color), BMP and TGA with Bgr24, PPM, QOI with IncludeAlpha = false. Frames after the first: JPEG, BMP, TGA, QOI and PNM. Metadata: every writer keeps what its format can carry; StripMetadata = true on any writer options drops it all. See the API reference for every option. What the file said Every reader fills RasterMetadata.FormatDetails with the header's own terms: PngDetails, JpegDetails, GifDetails, BmpDetails, TgaDetails, QoiDetails or PnmDetails. A writer of the same format uses them to keep what it can, and ignores another format's details. // Each reader fills in what the file's header says, in the format's own terms. using Raster png = Raster.Load("duck.png"); if (png.Metadata.FormatDetails is PngDetails pngDetails) { Console.WriteLine($"PNG {pngDetails.ColorType}, {pngDetails.BitDepth}-bit, interlaced: {pngDetails.Interlaced}"); foreach (PngTextSource source in pngDetails.TextSources) { Console.WriteLine($"Text from a {source.ChunkType} chunk, compressed: {source.Compressed}"); } } using Raster bmp = Raster.Load("duck.bmp"); BmpDetails bmpDetails = (BmpDetails)bmp.Metadata.FormatDetails!; Console.WriteLine($"BMP {bmpDetails.BitsPerPixel}-bit, {bmpDetails.Compression}, {bmpDetails.HeaderSize}-byte header"); using Raster tga = Raster.Load("duck.tga"); TgaDetails tgaDetails = (TgaDetails)tga.Metadata.FormatDetails!; Console.WriteLine($"TGA type {tgaDetails.ImageType}, origin {tgaDetails.Origin}, alpha {tgaDetails.AlphaType}"); using Raster qoi = Raster.Load("duck.qoi"); QoiDetails qoiDetails = (QoiDetails)qoi.Metadata.FormatDetails!; Console.WriteLine($"QOI {qoiDetails.Channels} channels, linear: {qoiDetails.Linear}"); using Raster pgm = Raster.Load("duck.pgm"); PnmDetails pnmDetails = (PnmDetails)pgm.Metadata.FormatDetails!; Console.WriteLine($"PNM {pnmDetails.Kind}, maxval {pnmDetails.MaxValue}, plain text: {pnmDetails.PlainText}"); More PNG and TGA writer settings: // Force a palette, choose a filter and a zlib strategy, and keep a private chunk. ((PngDetails)image.Metadata.FormatDetails!).OtherChunks.Add( new PngChunk("prVt", "hello"u8.ToArray(), PngChunkPosition.AfterImageData)); image.Save("duck-palette.png", new PngWriterOptions { ColorType = PngColorType.Palette, Filter = PngFilterMode.Paeth, CompressionStrategy = PngCompressionStrategy.Filtered, }); image.Save("duck-gray.tga", new TgaWriterOptions { PixelFormat = TgaPixelFormat.Gray8, Rle = false }); using Raster back = Raster.Load("duck-gray.tga"); TgaDetails details = (TgaDetails)back.Metadata.FormatDetails!; bool upsideDown = details.Origin is TgaOrigin.BottomLeft or TgaOrigin.BottomRight; bool hasAlpha = details.AlphaType is TgaAlphaType.Straight or TgaAlphaType.Premultiplied; Each format is described by a FormatInfo: its name, extensions, MIME types, and how to recognize it from its first bytes. // Every built-in format, with its name, extensions and MIME types; Raster.Save picks one by extension. foreach (FormatInfo format in new[] { PngFormat.Info, JpegFormat.Info, GifFormat.Info, BmpFormat.Info, TgaFormat.Info, QoiFormat.Info, PnmFormat.Info }) { Console.WriteLine($"{format.Name}: {string.Join(", ", format.Extensions)} ({string.Join(", ", format.MimeTypes)})"); } // A SignatureMatcher decides from the first SignatureLength bytes whether a file is in the format. SignatureMatcher isPng = PngFormat.Info.Matches; bool png = isPng(File.ReadAllBytes("duck.png").AsSpan(0, PngFormat.Info.SignatureLength)); Run it samples/Formats is a console app that does what this guide shows on the bundled images: dotnet run --project samples/Formats writes its results to ./output.

articles/guides/hdr.html.title: HDR files | Egami
articles/guides/hdr.html.summary: HDR files Egami reads and writes Radiance pictures (.hdr) and OpenEXR images (.exr), lists the images of Multi-Picture JPEG files, and reads, keeps and writes the gain maps of Ultra HDR, ISO 21496-1 and Apple JPEGs. HDR pixels load as linear light in floating point, unclamped, with 1.0 as reference white (203 cd/m²), the same scale the color management guide's tone mapping and HDR metadata use. Radiance Radiance pictures hold three 8-bit mantissas and a shared exponent per pixel (RGBE), or CIE X, Y and Z the same way (XYZE). RadianceFormat reads both, every scan order a resolution line can name (-Y 512 +X 768 and the other seven), and flat, old-style repeat-pixel and per-channel run-length scanlines. Pixels load as RgbF32, bit for bit what stb_image decodes; XYZE converts to RGB in Radiance's standard primaries, which RasterMetadata.Primaries then names. A PRIMARIES line sets the primaries of an RGBE file the same way; without one, Rec. 709 is assumed. RadianceDetails keeps the header: the RadiancePixelFormat, Exposure, ColorCorrection, Primaries, Software, View, PixelAspectRatio, the scan order as stored and every header line. The reader also measures the brightest value and stores it as HdrMetadata.MaxContentLightLevel, so ToneMap fits the image rather than a fixed 1,000 cd/m² peak. // Linear light, unclamped: 1.0 is reference white. The brightest value is measured as the light level ToneMap fits. using Raster<RgbF32> hdr = Raster.Load<RgbF32>("desk.hdr"); var details = (RadianceDetails)hdr.Metadata.FormatDetails!; double? exposure = details.Exposure; // the header's EXPOSURE lines; the pixels are kept as stored // To SDR: tone map, then save. Saving the HDR raster to PNG or JPEG as it is would clip the highlights. using Raster<RgbF32> mapped = hdr.Derive(ops => ops.ToneMap(ToneMapping.Bt2390)); mapped.Save("desk.jpg"); // RGBE with per-channel run-length scanlines, as Radiance writes them; EXPOSURE only when asked for. hdr.Save("copy.hdr"); hdr.Save("labeled.hdr", new RadianceWriterOptions { Exposure = 1.5 }); The writer writes RGBE, top row first, with per-channel run-length scanlines (RadianceWriterOptions.Compress = false writes them flat) and an EXPOSURE line only when RadianceWriterOptions.Exposure is set. Reading a file and writing it again gives the same floats, and the same bytes once written by Egami. OpenEXR ExrFormat reads scanline and tiled files, single and multi-part (ExrPartKind), with every compression of OpenEXR 3 (ExrCompression: NONE, RLE, ZIPS, ZIP, PIZ, PXR24, B44, B44A, DWAA and DWAB; HTJ2K is refused), half, float and uint channels (ExrPixelType), and luminance-chroma images. Pixels match OpenEXR's own decode bit for bit, DWA within one half-float step. A load gives the first part's R, G, B and A (or Y, YA or the luminance-chroma channels) as linear light; a tiled part loads its full-resolution level (ExrLevelMode says which levels it has). Deep parts throw UnsupportedFormatException. ExrDetails lists every part as an ExrPart: its name, channels (ExrChannel), layers, data and display windows, tile size, chromaticities and every header attribute as an ExrHeaderEntry. ExrReaderOptions picks the Part, a Layer (such as diffuse for diffuse.R, diffuse.G and diffuse.B) and the ExrWindow to load: the data window, the pixels the file stores (the default), or the display window, padded with transparent black where there is no data. ExrImage.ReadChannel loads any one channel, such as depth or an object id, as 32-bit float. // The first part's RGBA channels as linear light, 1.0 reference white; other layers by name. using Raster<RgbaF32> beauty = Raster.Load<RgbaF32>("render.exr"); var details = (ExrDetails)beauty.Metadata.FormatDetails!; IReadOnlyList<string> layers = details.Parts[details.Part].Layers; // "diffuse", "specular" using Raster<RgbaF32> diffuse = Raster.Load<RgbaF32>("render.exr", options: new ExrReaderOptions { Layer = "diffuse" }); // Any one channel, such as depth or an object id, as 32-bit float. using Raster<GrayF32> depth = ExrImage.ReadChannel("aov.exr", "Z"); The writer writes one scanline part with R, G, B and A when the raster has alpha (ExrWriterOptions): ZIP by default, or NONE, RLE, ZIPS or PIZ, in half or float (ExrWriterOptions.PixelType; by default float for float rasters other than RgbaF16, half otherwise). A non-linear raster, such as sRGB, is converted to linear light first, and primaries other than Rec. 709 are written as chromaticities. OpenEXR reads every file Egami writes to the same values. // Half-float RGBA, ZIP-compressed, by default; a sRGB or other non-linear raster is linearized first. beauty.Save("copy.exr"); beauty.Save("float.exr", new ExrWriterOptions { Compression = ExrCompression.Piz, PixelType = ExrPixelType.Float }); Multi-Picture JPEG files Phones store more than one image in a JPEG: a gain map for HDR, large previews, the second view of a stereo pair. The CIPA Multi-Picture Format (MPF) lists them in an APP2 segment. JpegDetails.MultiPicture gives that index as MpfData: an MpfImage for each image with its MpfImageType, flags, length, and offset from the start of the file (the same numbers ExifTool prints). Raster.Probe counts them in RasterInfo.ImageCount, and Raster.LoadAll loads each JPEG one, the primary first. A damaged index never fails a load: the primary loads with a Jpeg.MpfDamaged warning. // A JPEG's Multi-Picture index lists the images stored after the primary: previews, stereo views, a gain map. using Raster photo = Raster.Load("ultrahdr.jpg"); MpfData? index = ((JpegDetails)photo.Metadata.FormatDetails!).MultiPicture; foreach (MpfImage image in index?.Images ?? []) { Console.WriteLine($"{image.Type}: {image.Length:N0} bytes at {image.Offset:N0}"); } // LoadAll gives every JPEG image the index lists, the primary first; a plain JPEG gives one. using RasterList all = Raster.LoadAll("ultrahdr.jpg"); Gain maps An Ultra HDR JPEG, as Android phones, Chrome and Photoshop write it, is an SDR picture any viewer shows, followed (through MPF) by a gain map: how much brighter each part of the picture is in the HDR rendition. ISO 21496-1, Adobe's hdrgm XMP (Ultra HDR 1.0) and Apple's HDRGainMap are three ways of writing the same idea down; GainMapFormat says which a file used, and GainMapInfo holds its values, in log2 units as the standards give them. A load gives the SDR picture as stored, with the map in RasterMetadata.GainMap as a GainMap (GainMapValues per channel); a damaged map is dropped with Jpeg.GainMapDropped. ReaderOptions.Hdr asks for the HDR rendition instead: HdrDecode.Headroom is how much brighter than SDR white the display can go (or the map's full capacity), and the load gives linear RgbaF16, within about 1% of libultrahdr's decode. GainMap.Apply does the same for a raster in hand. // As stored: the SDR base image, with the gain map in the metadata. using Raster sdr = Raster.Load("ultrahdr.jpg"); GainMap? map = sdr.Metadata.GainMap; // null for a plain JPEG // The HDR rendition for a display 4x as bright as SDR white: linear half floats, 1.0 = SDR white. using Raster<RgbaF16> hdr = Raster.Load<RgbaF16>("ultrahdr.jpg", options: new ReaderOptions { Hdr = new HdrDecode { Headroom = 4 } }); // The same from a raster in hand, at the map's full capacity. using Raster<RgbaF16> full = map!.Apply(sdr); Saving as JPEG writes the map back, in both metadata forms, as Skia and libultrahdr write them. Crops, turns, flips and resizes move the map with the picture; operations that change pixel values drop it (Operation.GainMapDropped), as do other formats (Save.GainMapDropped) and JpegWriterOptions.KeepGainMap = false. // Crops, turns, flips and resizes move the gain map with the picture; saving as JPEG writes it back. using Raster photo = Raster.Load("ultrahdr.jpg"); using Raster cropped = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Crop(16, 16, 200, 150).Rotate(90)); cropped.Save("cropped.jpg"); // still Ultra HDR // Operations that change pixel values drop it (Operation.GainMapDropped), and so do formats other than JPEG // (Save.GainMapDropped); KeepGainMap = false leaves it out on purpose. cropped.Save("sdr-only.jpg", new JpegWriterOptions { KeepGainMap = false }); To write an HDR raster as Ultra HDR, set JpegWriterOptions.GainMap: the raster is tone mapped to the SDR picture and GainMap.Create makes the map that brings it back. GainMapOptions has libultrahdr's defaults (a full-size, color map, gamma 1, quality 95) and each can be changed; Create also takes an SDR rendition you graded yourself. // An HDR raster as Ultra HDR: the SDR base, tone mapped with BT.2390, and a gain map that brings the HDR raster back. using Raster<RgbaF32> hdr = Raster.Load<RgbaF32>("render.exr"); hdr.Save("render.jpg", new JpegWriterOptions { Quality = 90, GainMap = new GainMapOptions() }); // Or choose the SDR rendition: the map goes in its metadata, and saving as JPEG writes both. using Raster<Rgb8> sdr = hdr.Derive(ops => ops.ToneMap(ToneMapping.Reinhard)).As<Rgb8>(); sdr.Metadata.GainMap = GainMap.Create(hdr, sdr, new GainMapOptions { Scale = 4 }); sdr.Save("graded.jpg", new JpegWriterOptions { Quality = 90 }); Saving HDR to an SDR format PNG, JPEG and the other 8 and 16-bit formats hold 0 to 1. Saving a floating-point raster to them clamps, as other libraries do; when the raster holds light above reference white, the save also reports Save.HdrClipped, naming ToneMap, which rolls the highlights off instead of cutting them.

articles/guides/ico.html.title: ICO and CUR | Egami
articles/guides/ico.html.summary: ICO and CUR Egami reads and writes Windows icons (.ico) and cursors (.cur), written from Microsoft's documentation of the icon directory. IcoFormat.Info and CurFormat.Info are registered in EgamiContext.Default. An icon holds several images, its entries, each a whole PNG file or a BMP without its file header; Egami's own PNG and BMP readers decode them, so an entry loads exactly as the same PNG or BMP would. Every entry of the test corpus decodes as ImageMagick and Pillow decode it, and the icons Egami writes open in ImageMagick, Pillow, SkiaSharp and Windows' own decoder (WIC) with the same pixels. Reading icons Raster.Load returns the best entry: the largest, then the deepest (a PNG entry counts as 32 bits), then the first. SkiaSharp picks the same entry, except that among entries of the largest size it takes the first where Egami takes the deepest, as Windows prefers. Raster.LoadAll returns every entry at its own size, in the file's order, and Raster.Probe lists them from the directory without decoding a pixel: RasterInfo.ImageCount, and IcoDetails.Entries on a loaded raster. // Load gives the best entry: the largest, then the deepest. LoadAll gives every entry at its own size. using Raster best = Raster.Load("app.ico"); using RasterList entries = Raster.LoadAll("app.ico"); // MinimumSize picks the smallest entry at least that big, so a 32 × 32 toolbar icon decodes only the 32 × 32 entry. using Raster small = Raster.Load("app.ico", options: new ReaderOptions { MinimumSize = new Size(32, 32) }); ReaderOptions.MinimumSize picks the smallest entry at least that big before the reduction rule applies to it, so a 32 × 32 request from a 16, 32, 48 and 256 icon decodes only the 32 × 32 entry. IcoReaderOptions.Entry names an entry by its index in the directory. // Pick an entry by its place in the file's directory. using Raster second = Raster.Load("app.ico", options: new IcoReaderOptions { Entry = 1 }); // Probe reads only the directory: the sizes an icon holds, without decoding a pixel. RasterInfo info = Raster.Probe("app.ico"); Console.WriteLine($"{info.ImageCount} entries; Load gives {info.Width}×{info.Height}"); using Raster best = Raster.Load("app.ico"); foreach (IcoEntry entry in ((IcoDetails)best.Metadata.FormatDetails!).Entries) { Console.WriteLine($"{entry.Width}×{entry.Height}, {entry.BitsPerPixel} bits, {entry.Encoding}"); } Every entry loads as Rgba8. BMP entries at 1, 4, 8, 16, 24 and 32 bits are read, with palettes and bit fields; the 1-bit AND mask after the color rows makes pixels transparent. At 32 bits the alpha channel wins, as in Windows, except that an alpha channel of 0 everywhere, which old writers left, falls back to the mask; ImageMagick, Pillow and SkiaSharp keep such an entry fully transparent instead. The directory's sizes and depths are hints: the entry's own header wins, with the Ico.DirectoryMismatch warning. A cursor's entries carry IcoDetails.Hotspot. Writing icons Saving one raster writes one entry at its own size; a raster larger than 256 is fitted to 256 with the Save.IcoFitted warning. IcoWriterOptions.Sizes writes a set instead, each size resized from the largest raster given with Filter, or taken as drawn from a raster of exactly that size; FaviconSizes (16, 32, 48) and WindowsSizes (16, 24, 32, 48, 64, 256) are ready-made. A raster that is not square is fitted inside each square and centred on transparency. // A favicon: 16, 32 and 48 resized from one raster. A raster that is not square is centred on transparency. logo.Save("favicon.ico", new IcoWriterOptions { Sizes = IcoWriterOptions.FaviconSizes }); // Windows' set: 16 to 256, the 256 entry as PNG and the rest as 32-bit BMP, as Microsoft's guidance asks. logo.Save("app.ico", new IcoWriterOptions { Sizes = IcoWriterOptions.WindowsSizes, Filter = Egami.Operations.ResampleFilter.Lanczos3 }); // Hand-drawn small sizes: each raster is written at its own size; the 48 comes from the largest raster. using Raster<Rgba8> drawn16 = logo.Derive(ops => ops.Fit(16, 16)); Raster.SaveAll([logo, drawn16], "drawn.ico", new IcoWriterOptions { Sizes = [16, 48] }); IcoWriterOptions.Encoding, an IcoEntryEncoding, forces every entry to PNG or BMP. Left null, the default, it writes 256 × 256 entries as PNG and smaller ones as 32-bit BMP with an AND mask built from alpha, as Microsoft's guidance asks; a raster loaded from an icon and written at its own size keeps its entry's kind. PNG entries are always 8-bit RGBA, the only kind Windows lists. Entries are sorted smallest first, two entries of one size throw ArgumentException, and the same rasters and options give the same bytes. Pixels are written at 8 bits; an ICC profile goes into PNG entries, while EXIF, XMP and IPTC are not written and a warning says so. Cursors are icons with a hotspot: IcoWriterOptions.Hotspot gives it at the raster's own size, scaled to each entry and kept inside it; without it, a raster loaded from a cursor keeps its hotspot. // A cursor is an icon with a hotspot, given at the raster's own size and scaled to each entry. arrow.Save("pointer.cur", new IcoWriterOptions { Sizes = [32, 48], Hotspot = new Point(0, 0) }); using RasterList cursor = Raster.LoadAll("pointer.cur"); Point? hotspot = ((IcoDetails)cursor[0].Metadata.FormatDetails!).Hotspot; Speed An icon is read whole, since its directory points anywhere in it. On the 256 × 256 PNG entry Egami decodes faster than SkiaSharp, and 24 and 32-bit BMP entries go straight into place, twice as fast as SkiaSharp; writing Windows' six sizes from a 256 × 256 image takes half the time ImageMagick (Magick.NET) does. Damaged and hostile data The entry count is checked against SafetyLimits.MaxFrames and every entry's size against the other limits before its pixels are allocated; every offset and size is checked against the file. In strict mode an entry that lies outside the file, overlaps another or is neither PNG nor BMP throws CorruptDataException; in lenient mode it is skipped with the Ico.EntrySkipped warning, and the load fails only when no entry is left. A BMP entry that ends before its mask loads with the missing rows opaque (Ico.MaskMissing). The reader is fuzzed with AFL++ through whole files and through single entries.

articles/guides/jbig2.html.title: JBIG2 | Egami
articles/guides/jbig2.html.summary: JBIG2 Egami reads JBIG2 (ITU-T T.88 | ISO/IEC 14492), the bi-level format of scanned documents and of the JBIG2Decode images in PDF, written from the 2018 edition of T.88 and the PDF specification. Jbig2Format.Info is registered in EgamiContext.Default. JBIG2 is never written. Every page of Egami's corpus (made with jbig2enc in each of its modes), of PDFBox's JBIG2 test streams and of the T.88 Annex H datastream decodes bit for bit as PDFium and jbig2dec decode it. Reading files A standalone file starts with the T.88 file header, so Raster.Load recognizes it. Each page loads as Gray8: black 0, white 255, as 1-bit TIFF does. Load reads the first page, or the one Jbig2ReaderOptions.Page names; LoadAll reads every page at its own size, and RasterInfo.ImageCount says how many there are without decoding any. // A standalone .jb2 file is detected like any other format; each page loads as Gray8, black 0 and white 255. using Raster first = Raster.Load("book.jb2"); using RasterList pages = Raster.LoadAll("book.jb2"); using Raster third = Raster.Load("book.jb2", options: new Jbig2ReaderOptions { Page = 2 }); Images from a PDF A PDF holds JBIG2 in T.88's embedded form: segments without a file header, and often a separate JBIG2Globals stream with the symbol dictionaries several images share. The embedded form has no signature, so load it with the format named. Jbig2Globals.Parse decodes the globals once; the object is immutable and can be shared by every image of the document, on any thread. // A PDF's JBIG2Decode image has no file header, so name the format. Parse the JBIG2Globals stream once and share it: // every image of the document that refers to it reuses its decoded symbols. Jbig2Globals globals = Jbig2Globals.Parse(globalsStream); using Raster image = Raster.Load(imageStream, Jbig2Format.Info, options: new Jbig2ReaderOptions { Globals = globals }); A PDF image's /Decode array and its color space stay the PDF library's business: Egami returns the page as T.88 defines it. What is decoded Segment Read Generic regions Templates 0 to 3 and the extended template, adaptive pixels anywhere, typical prediction, skipped pixels; MMR through Egami's CCITT Group 4 decoder Refinement regions Templates 0 and 1, typical prediction, against the page or an intermediate region Symbol dictionaries, text regions Arithmetic and Huffman, refinement and aggregation, every reference corner and transposition, standard tables B.1 to B.15 and code table segments Pattern dictionaries, halftone regions Arithmetic and MMR gray-scale planes, any grid, skipping Pages Known and unknown height, striped, every combination operator, intermediate regions; end of file and random-access files Extensions Comments into Jbig2Details.Comments; others skipped unless marked necessary, which throws NotSupportedException Colour palettes (T.88 Amendment 3) Skipped with a warning; the page decodes as bilevel Jbig2Details reports, per page, the stream's Jbig2Organization, whether the page used the globals, its striping, default pixel and Jbig2CombinationOperator, the Jbig2RegionKinds it is made of and whether it is eventually lossless. The page information's resolution goes to RasterMetadata.Resolution. using Raster page = Raster.Load("book.jb2"); var details = (Jbig2Details)page.Metadata.FormatDetails!; Console.WriteLine($"Page {details.PageIndex}, {details.Organization}, regions {details.Regions}"); Console.WriteLine($"Default pixel {details.DefaultPixel}, combined by {details.CombinationOperator}, lossless {details.Lossless}"); Damaged and hostile data JBIG2 decoders are a long-standing attack surface (FORCEDENTRY, in 2021, was an integer overflow in one), so every size is checked arithmetic and counted against SafetyLimits before memory is taken: page and region sizes against MaxWidth, MaxHeight and MaxPixels; symbols, patterns, tables and every bitmap together against MaxTotalBytes. A segment that refers to a segment that is not before it, in the stream or in the globals, always throws. In lenient mode a damaged region is skipped with a warning and the rest of the page decodes; strict mode throws CorruptDataException. The ITU's own conformance streams for T.88 mostly break the Recommendation (their text regions refer to no symbol dictionary), and PDFium and jbig2dec reject them as Egami does; the two that follow it, and the Annex H datastream, decode exactly.

articles/guides/jpeg.html.title: JPEG | Egami
articles/guides/jpeg.html.summary: JPEG JPEG files load like any other: baseline, extended and progressive, Huffman or arithmetic-coded, gray, YCbCr, RGB, CMYK and YCCK, any chroma subsampling. The decoded pixels match libjpeg-turbo's djpeg exactly. Arithmetic, 12-bit and lossless files Arithmetic-coded files load like Huffman-coded ones. 12-bit files load in their natural 16-bit types (Gray16, Rgb16, or Cmyk16 for four components), each sample scaled so 4095 becomes 65535; ask for an 8-bit type and they are rounded to it. Lossless JPEG, the kind inside DNG tiles and many DICOM files, decodes to its exact samples at 2 to 16 bits: up to 8 bits as Gray8 or Rgb8, deeper as Gray16 or Rgb16. Three-component lossless files are RGB unless a JFIF segment or Adobe transform says YCbCr. Lossless files have no DCT, so MinimumSize reduces them after a full decode. JpegDetails.Precision, Arithmetic and Lossless say what a file is. Hierarchical files are refused with UnsupportedFormatException. Browsers show none of these modes. Egami writes 12-bit files on request (below), but no arithmetic or lossless ones. Threads A large file decodes on up to MaxParallelism threads with the same pixels as one thread. A file with restart markers is split at the markers already in it; a progressive file's scans run as a pipeline, each refinement scan a few rows behind the scan before it, and the last pass is split by rows. A sequential file without markers overlaps its entropy decoding with the rest on a second thread. Damaged data falls back to one thread, so warnings and recovery are as before. Scaled decode // At least 100 × 75 from the stored JPEG, decoded at 1/2, 1/4 or 1/8 scale straight from the DCT. using Raster preview = Raster.Load("duck.jpg", options: new ReaderOptions { MinimumSize = new Size(100, 75) }); ReaderOptions.MinimumSize picks the smallest of 1/1, 1/2, 1/4 and 1/8 scale that still covers the size you need, and decodes at that scale straight from the DCT. For a thumbnail from a 12-megapixel photo it is many times faster than decoding in full and resizing. Other formats ignore it. Orientation Cameras and phones store pixels as the sensor saw them and say in EXIF how to turn them. Raster.Probe reports the orientation, and AutoOrient applies it; see resizing and geometry. To turn the file itself upright without re-encoding it, use JpegTransform with AutoOrient (see lossless rotation). Writing using FileStream output = File.Create("duck-q85.jpg"); image.Save(output, JpegFormat.Info, new JpegWriterOptions { Quality = 85, // 75 by default, on libjpeg's scale Subsampling = ChromaSubsampling.Subsample444, // 4:2:0 by default OptimizeHuffman = true, // a few percent smaller, a little slower }); Option Default Does Quality 75 1 to 100, the same scale as libjpeg's cjpeg Subsampling Subsample420 Subsample422 or Subsample444 keep more color detail OptimizeHuffman false Tables built for the image: a few percent smaller ColorType Auto Gray writes one gray component whatever the pixel type; Cmyk and Ycck write four (Auto picks Cmyk for CMYK pixels) Progressive false Scans that show a coarse image first and refine it, with tables optimized per scan Precision 8 12 keeps more of 16-bit and float pixels RestartInterval 0 Restart markers every so many blocks, for damaged-stream recovery Background none Composites alpha onto this color first; without it alpha is ignored Progressive // Shows coarse first and sharpens as it loads; usually a few percent smaller, and decodes to the same pixels. image.Save("duck-progressive.jpg", new JpegWriterOptions { Progressive = true }); Progressive writes the scan script libjpeg's cjpeg -progressive writes: ten scans for color, six for gray, spectral selection and successive approximation, each scan with its own optimized Huffman tables. The file decodes to exactly the pixels the baseline file at the same quality gives, and is the same file cjpeg -progressive writes. The encoder holds every quantized coefficient until the last scan, about 2 bytes per sample (72 MB for a 24-megapixel 4:2:0 photo), counted against SafetyLimits.MaxTotalBytes; a streamed encode buffers them. Re-saving a progressive file writes baseline unless you set it. CMYK and YCCK // CMYK pixels save as CMYK, inverted behind an Adobe marker as Photoshop writes; YCCK is usually smaller. using Raster<Cmyk8> inks = image.As<Cmyk8>(); inks.Save("duck-cmyk-out.jpg", JpegWriterOptions.Default); inks.Save("duck-ycck.jpg", new JpegWriterOptions { ColorType = JpegColorType.Ycck }); Cmyk8 and Cmyk16 pixels save as four CMYK components with an Adobe marker, the values inverted as Photoshop writes them and every reader expects, and no JFIF segment (JFIF covers gray and YCbCr only). Ycck converts cyan, magenta and yellow to YCbCr as libjpeg does and subsamples their chroma by Subsampling, keeping black at full size; it is usually smaller. Other pixel types written as Cmyk or Ycck are converted with the plain formula. djpeg, ImageMagick and Pillow read the files to the same inks. 12-bit // 16-bit and float pixels keep more than 8 bits in a 12-bit file; it loads back as Rgb16. No browser shows it. using Raster<Rgb16> deep = image.As<Rgb16>(); deep.Save("duck-12bit.jpg", new JpegWriterOptions { Precision = 12, Quality = 95 }); Precision = 12 writes 12-bit samples (an extended, SOF1 file, or SOF2 when progressive) from any pixel type, narrowing 16-bit samples to 12 bits; it is worth it for 16-bit and float pixels. The Huffman tables are always optimized, as libjpeg-turbo does at 12 bits, and quantization tables pass 255 at low quality, in 16-bit entries. libjpeg-turbo's djpeg reads them; browsers, Pillow and many ImageMagick builds do not. Lossless rotation, flips and crops // Turns the photo upright by its EXIF orientation without re-encoding: no quality is lost, and the tag is reset. JpegTransform.Apply("sideways.jpg", "upright.jpg", new JpegTransformOptions { Operation = JpegTransformOperation.AutoOrient }); // Rotates, crops and drops the color in one pass; a file can be transformed in place. JpegTransformResult result = JpegTransform.Apply("upright.jpg", "upright.jpg", new JpegTransformOptions { Operation = JpegTransformOperation.Rotate90, Crop = new Rect(0, 0, 200, 120), Grayscale = true, }); Console.WriteLine($"{result.Width} × {result.Height}"); JpegTransform turns, mirrors, crops and drops the color of a JPEG without decoding it to pixels, as jpegtran does: the quantized DCT coefficients move and change sign block by block, and are coded again, so the result has exactly the quality the file had. Quantization tables and chroma subsampling stay as they were. It takes every mode the reader takes except lossless JPEG: baseline, progressive, arithmetic (written back with Huffman coding), 12-bit, gray, CMYK and YCCK. The result decodes to the same pixels as the file jpegtran makes with the same switches, on every subsampling and edge case. Option Default Does Operation None FlipHorizontal, FlipVertical, Rotate90, Rotate180, Rotate270, Transpose, Transverse, or AutoOrient: what the EXIF orientation needs, then the tag is reset to normal Crop none The area to keep, after the operation; its top-left corner moves to the MCU grid (8 or 16 pixels), as jpegtran -crop does Grayscale false Keeps only luma: a gray file with no loss. YCbCr files only Edges Trim What happens at a mirrored edge that is not a whole number of MCUs (below) Progressive false Writes progressive scans, as JpegWriterOptions.Progressive does OptimizeHuffman true Tables built for the result, a few percent smaller than the standard ones CopyMetadata true Copies EXIF, ICC, XMP, IPTC, comments and other segments A block of 8 × 8 pixels moves as a whole, so an edge that is not a whole number of MCUs (8 pixels, or 16 with subsampled chroma) cannot be mirrored to the other side intact. JpegTransformEdges.Trim drops that partial MCU from each mirrored edge, so the image loses up to 15 pixels there, as jpegtran -trim does; Strict throws instead, as -perfect does; Keep leaves it in place unmirrored, as jpegtran does by default. Edges that are not mirrored keep every pixel, and Transpose never loses any. EXIF's pixel dimensions follow the result, and its thumbnail gets the same rotation, flip and gray conversion; after a crop the thumbnail is dropped, since it would still show the whole picture. An MPF index (the extra images some cameras append) is dropped too. Other segments are copied byte for byte. The result's size and any warnings about a damaged source are in the returned JpegTransformResult. The whole image's coefficients are held while it runs, about 2 bytes per sample, counted against SafetyLimits.MaxTotalBytes. A 12-megapixel photo turns in 170 ms with optimized tables (jpegtran -optimize: 305 ms), 130 ms with the standard ones (jpegtran: 246 ms) and 260 ms written progressive (jpegtran: 458 ms). What the file says using Raster image = Raster.Load("duck.jpg"); if (image.Metadata.FormatDetails is JpegDetails jpeg) { Console.WriteLine($"Progressive: {jpeg.Progressive}, saved at about quality {jpeg.EstimatedQuality}"); } EXIF, XMP (including extended XMP) and ICC profiles are read and written back. A JPEG saved again is re-encoded: pixels lose a little each time, so keep a lossless master if you edit repeatedly, or use JpegTransform for rotations, flips and crops. Details The components, color space and estimated quality are in JpegDetails. JpegReaderOptions.FastUpsampling trades a little chroma sharpness for speed; JpegColorType.Gray writes one channel. CMYK and YCCK files load as RGB by the plain formula, R = (1 − C)(1 − K). Raster.Load<Cmyk8> returns the file's ink amounts instead, without the RGB step; print-accurate color needs the embedded ICC profile, which Egami keeps but does not apply yet. using Raster photo = Raster.Load("duck.jpg", options: new JpegReaderOptions { FastUpsampling = true }); JpegDetails details = (JpegDetails)photo.Metadata.FormatDetails!; Console.WriteLine($"{details.ColorSpace}, progressive: {details.Progressive}, quality about {details.EstimatedQuality}"); foreach (JpegComponent component in details.Components) { Console.WriteLine($"Component {component.Id}: sampled {component.HorizontalSampling} × {component.VerticalSampling}"); } // Gray output, and 4:4:4 (no chroma subsampling) for sharp colored edges. photo.Save("gray.jpg", new JpegWriterOptions { ColorType = JpegColorType.Gray }); photo.Save("sharp.jpg", new JpegWriterOptions { Quality = 90, Subsampling = ChromaSubsampling.Subsample444 }); Run it samples/Jpeg is a console app that does what this guide shows on the bundled images: dotnet run --project samples/Jpeg writes its results to ./output.

articles/guides/jpeg2000.html.title: JPEG 2000 | Egami
articles/guides/jpeg2000.html.summary: JPEG 2000 Egami reads JPEG 2000 (ITU-T T.800 | ISO/IEC 15444-1, all of Part 1), written from the 2019 edition of T.800, T.801's JPX boxes and the PDF specification's JPXDecode filter. Jpeg2000Format.Info is registered in EgamiContext.Default; JPEG 2000 is never written. Every ISO/IEC 15444-4 conformance codestream decodes within its tolerances: the reversible ones to OpenJPEG 2.5.4's samples exactly, the irreversible ones within one level, at full resolution and with levels dropped. Reading files JP2 and JPX files start with the JP2 signature box and raw codestreams (J2K, J2C, a PDF's JPXDecode stream) with SOC and SIZ, so Raster.Load recognizes both. MinimumSize drops whole wavelet levels, JPEG 2000's own reduction (a quarter of the levels' work for each level dropped), and Region decodes only the tiles and code-blocks the rectangle needs, so a thumbnail of a large scan or a viewport into a map costs a fraction of the whole decode. Rows stream a row of tiles at a time. // JP2, JPX and raw codestreams are detected like any other format, so is a PDF's JPXDecode stream. using Raster photo = Raster.Load("photo.jp2"); // A thumbnail drops whole wavelet levels instead of decoding at full size, and a region decodes only the code-blocks // it needs. using Raster thumbnail = Raster.Load("photo.jp2", options: new ReaderOptions { MinimumSize = new Size(24, 18) }); using Raster corner = Raster.Load("photo.jp2", options: new ReaderOptions { Region = new Rect(0, 0, 32, 32) }); What it loads as Jpeg2000ReaderOptions.Components chooses between two readings of the same samples. Jpeg2000Components Pixels Color (default) Palettes applied, channels placed by the channel definitions, sYCC and CIELab converted to sRGB; gray, RGB or CMYK, with alpha when a channel is opacity Raw The codestream's components after its own component transform: 1 as gray, 2 as gray and alpha, 3 as RGB, 4 as CMYK, for a PDF that names its own color space Depths widen to the next Egami type by bit replication, so the stored value is recoverable by a shift: 1 to 8 bits load as Gray8, Rgb8, Rgba8 or Cmyk8, 9 to 16 bits as their 16-bit forms, deeper ones as float types. Signed samples are offset by half their range, with the Jpeg2000.SignedSamples warning. Premultiplied alpha loads straight. ICC profiles go to RasterMetadata.IccProfile and the pixels stay as stored, as for every format; XMP, the resolution box and COM markers are read. Subsampled sYCC (4:2:0 and 4:2:2) is upsampled with the YUV kernels at JPEG 2000's chroma siting, or loads straight into a YuvRaster without upsampling; FastUpsampling repeats chroma as OpenJPEG does instead. MaxQualityLayers decodes only the first layers of a layered file, for a quick preview. // A PDF that names its own color space wants the codestream's components as stored. using Raster components = Raster.Load(jpxStream, options: new Jpeg2000ReaderOptions { Components = Jpeg2000Components.Raw }); // A quick preview of a layered file: only its first quality layer, chroma repeated as OpenJPEG does. using Raster preview = Raster.Load("photo.jp2", options: new Jpeg2000ReaderOptions { MaxQualityLayers = 1, FastUpsampling = true }); What is decoded Part Read Codestream SIZ, COD, COC, QCD, QCC, RGN, POC, PPM, PPT and COM; TLM, PLM, PLT and CRG read past; SOP and EPH; tiles and tile-parts in any order Tier 2 Packet headers with tag trees, all five progression orders, progression order changes, precincts of any size, packed packet headers Tier 1 The three coding passes and every code-block style: arithmetic bypass, context reset, termination on each pass, vertically causal contexts, predictable termination, segmentation symbols; ROI by max-shift Reconstruction Reversible 5/3 and irreversible 9/7 wavelets at any number of levels, odd sizes and offsets; RCT and ICT; subsampled and signed components JP2 and JPX ihdr, colr (enumerated, restricted and any ICC), pclr, cmap, cdef, res, XMP uuid; JPX's several colr boxes and rreq; the first codestream Refused Part 2 coding tools and High-Throughput (Part 15) code-blocks throw NotSupportedException naming the feature Jpeg2000Details describes what was decoded: the Jpeg2000Container, the profile, each Jpeg2000Component's precision, sign and sampling, the wavelet, levels, layers and Jpeg2000ProgressionOrder, the tiling, the Jpeg2000ColorSpace, whether there is a palette, the Jpeg2000Channel definitions with their Jpeg2000ChannelType, and the comments. using Raster image = Raster.Load("photo.jp2"); var details = (Jpeg2000Details)image.Metadata.FormatDetails!; Console.WriteLine($"{details.Container}, {(details.Reversible ? "lossless 5/3" : "lossy 9/7")}, {details.DecompositionLevels} levels"); Console.WriteLine($"{details.QualityLayers} layers in {details.ProgressionOrder} order, {details.TileCount} tiles, {details.ColorSpace}"); foreach (Jpeg2000Component component in details.Components) { Console.WriteLine($"{component.Precision} bits{(component.IsSigned ? " signed" : "")}, sampled every {component.SubsamplingX}×{component.SubsamplingY}"); } foreach (Jpeg2000Channel channel in details.Channels) { Console.WriteLine($"Channel {channel.Channel}: {channel.Type} for color {channel.Association}"); } Speed and threads Code-blocks are independent, so tier 1 runs across cores by EgamiContext.MaxParallelism, with the same output at any thread count; the wavelets and color conversions are vectorized. On a 10-megapixel photo Egami decodes lossy files faster than OpenJPEG on one thread and every file two to four times faster on all cores. Damaged and hostile data Every size in SIZ is checked against SafetyLimits before a tile is read; the number of tiles, components, levels, passes and packet lengths are bounded by the standard and by the data; the samples held count against MaxTotalBytes, and a codestream whose tiles and components would build far more structure than its samples fill is refused. A codestream that ends early decodes what it holds with the Jpeg2000.Truncated warning, and throws CorruptDataException in strict mode.

articles/guides/jxl.html.title: JPEG XL | Egami
articles/guides/jxl.html.summary: JPEG XL Egami reads and writes JPEG XL (ISO/IEC 18181), written from the specification with no native code. JxlFormat.Info is registered in EgamiContext.Default, so Raster.Load recognizes a bare codestream (FF 0A) or the box format from the first bytes, and Save("x.jxl") picks the writer. JxlDetails describes the container. Raster.Probe reads the headers alone: size, sample format, channels, orientation and frame count. // The headers alone: size, natural pixel type, orientation and frame count, without decoding any pixels. RasterInfo info = Raster.Probe("duck.jxl"); bool isJxl = info.Format == JxlFormat.Info; long bytes = info.EstimatedBytes; // what a full load would allocate Reading Every kind of still decodes: Lossless Modular: every predictor, RCT, palette and squeeze, 1 to 31-bit and float samples, alpha. Lossy VarDCT or Modular in XYB: every transform size, Gaborish, the edge-preserving filter, LF frames, upsampling, patches, splines and noise. // JPEG XL loads like any format: lossless, lossy, animated or recompressed from a JPEG, in its natural pixel type. using Raster duck = Raster.Load("duck.jxl"); duck.Save("duck.png"); The natural pixel type follows the bit depth: Rgb8, Rgba8 or Gray8, their 16-bit forms, RgbaF16 for 16-bit float, and RgbF32, RgbaF32 or GrayF32 beyond. CMYK loads as Cmyk8 or Cmyk16. Color: lossy (XYB) files come out in the file's own color space, enumerated (as djxl gives it) or from its ICC profile through Egami's color pipeline, and that space goes on the raster. PQ and HLG files keep their curve, named by H.273 code points, with intensity_target as HdrMetadata.MaxContentLightLevel; converting to sRGB as they load tone maps them: // An HDR (PQ or HLG) file, tone mapped into sRGB as it loads; the peak comes from the file's intensity_target. using Raster<Rgb8> sdr = Raster.Load<Rgb8>("hdr.jxl", options: new ReaderOptions { ConvertColorTo = Egami.Colors.ColorProfile.Srgb }); sdr.Save("hdr-as-sdr.jpg"); A jhgm gain map loads into RasterMetadata.GainMap, and ReaderOptions.Hdr renders HDR from it as for Ultra HDR JPEGs (see the HDR guide). Groups decode on several threads (EgamiContext.MaxParallelism), and ReaderOptions.Region on a still decodes only the groups it touches. JxlReaderOptions adds three choices on top of the general reader options: Option Default Does MaxDownscale 1 8 or more decodes only a lossy still's LF image, an eighth of the size each way and far faster RenderSpotColors true Mixes spot color channels into the color as djxl does; false leaves the color as coded LinearOutput false Gives linear light in float, in the file's own primaries, instead of its encoded color space Animations, layers and previews Animations load as their blended frames with delays and loop count. JxlImage.ReadLayers gives the frames before blending, each a JxlLayer with its offset, duration and JxlLayerBlend mode, for an editor; JxlImage.ReadPreview gives the preview a file may carry. // An animation loads as its frames, blended onto the canvas, each with its delay. using Raster animation = Raster.Load("sprite.jxl"); int frames = animation.FrameCount; // The layers before blending, for an editor: each at its own size and place. IReadOnlyList<JxlLayer> layers = JxlImage.ReadLayers("sprite.jxl"); foreach (JxlLayer layer in layers) { Console.WriteLine($"{layer.Raster.Width}x{layer.Raster.Height} at {layer.X},{layer.Y}: {layer.Blend}, {layer.Duration.TotalMilliseconds} ms"); layer.Dispose(); } // The preview some files carry for quick display, or null. using Raster? preview = JxlImage.ReadPreview("duck.jxl"); // A lossy still at an eighth of its size, from its LF image alone. using Raster thumbnail = Raster.Load("duck.jxl", options: new JxlReaderOptions { MaxDownscale = 8 }); Extra channels Alpha loads straight (premultiplied color is divided out). JxlDetails.ExtraChannels lists every channel as a JxlExtraChannel with its JxlExtraChannelKind (alpha, depth, spot color, selection mask and others), and JxlImage.ReadExtraChannel reads any one alone as gray floats. // Alpha joins the pixels (straight, even when the file premultiplies); other extra channels are listed in the details. using Raster image = Raster.Load("sprite.jxl"); JxlDetails details = (JxlDetails)image.Metadata.FormatDetails!; foreach (JxlExtraChannel channel in details.ExtraChannels) { Console.WriteLine($"{channel.Kind} '{channel.Name}', {channel.BitsPerSample} bits"); } // Any one of them alone, such as depth or a selection mask, as gray floats. using Raster<GrayF32> alpha = JxlImage.ReadExtraChannel("sprite.jxl", 0); // Spot colors are mixed into the color as djxl does, unless turned off. using Raster plain = Raster.Load("sprite.jxl", options: new JxlReaderOptions { RenderSpotColors = false }); Recompressed JPEGs JPEG XL can hold a JPEG losslessly, about a fifth smaller. JxlImage.RecompressJpeg makes such a file from a JPEG, and JxlImage.ReconstructJpeg gives the original back byte for byte. JxlDetails.HasJpegReconstruction says which files can. // A JPEG becomes a JPEG XL file about a fifth smaller with the same pixels, and comes back byte for byte. JxlImage.RecompressJpeg("duck.jpg", "duck.jxl"); JxlImage.ReconstructJpeg("duck.jxl", "duck-again.jpg"); Such files also load as pixels like any other: // A JPEG recompressed into JPEG XL loads as pixels like any other file, and gives its JPEG back byte for byte. using Raster image = Raster.Load("recompressed.jxl"); if (((JxlDetails)image.Metadata.FormatDetails!).HasJpegReconstruction) { JxlImage.ReconstructJpeg("recompressed.jxl", "original.jpg"); } Writing The writer makes lossless Modular files in the raster's own precision, or lossy VarDCT files in XYB, with ICC, EXIF, XMP and orientation. JxlWriterOptions follows cjxl's own knobs, so the same numbers give about the same files: Option Default Does Lossless null true writes Modular, false VarDCT; null keeps the kind of the JPEG XL file the raster came from and writes lossy otherwise Effort 5 1 (fastest) to 7 (smallest), cjxl's -e, for both kinds Quality 90 Lossy quality, 0 to 100, cjxl's -q scale; 90 is distance 1.0, visually lossless Distance null A distance as cjxl's -d instead of a quality, 0.1 to 25 AlphaDistance 0 Lossy files: 0 keeps alpha exact, larger values code it lossy KeepTransparentColors true Lossy files keep the color under fully transparent pixels; false gives smaller files Progressive false Lossy files as cjxl -p makes them: a coarse image first that sharpens PhotonNoiseIso null Film-like noise the decoder adds, as cjxl's --photon_noise_iso // Lossless JPEG XL, about the size cjxl -d 0 makes at the same effort (1 fastest to 7 smallest, 5 by default). using Raster photo = Raster.Load("duck.png"); photo.Save("duck-lossless.jxl", new JxlWriterOptions { Lossless = true, Effort = 7 }); // Lossy JPEG XL at cjxl's default: quality 90, which is distance 1.0 (visually lossless). using Raster photo = Raster.Load("duck.png"); photo.Save("duck-lossy.jxl", new JxlWriterOptions { Lossless = false }); // A distance as cjxl -d takes it instead of a quality, and more effort for a smaller file. photo.Save("duck-small.jxl", new JxlWriterOptions { Lossless = false, Distance = 2.5f, Effort = 7 }); // Alpha stays exact in lossy files by default, and fully transparent pixels keep their color. using Raster<Rgba8> logo = Raster.Load<Rgba8>("duck.png"); logo.Save("logo.jxl", new JxlWriterOptions { Lossless = false, Quality = 85 }); // Smaller: alpha coded lossy too, and the color under transparent pixels left to the encoder (as cjxl does). logo.Save("logo-small.jxl", new JxlWriterOptions { Lossless = false, AlphaDistance = 1, KeepTransparentColors = false });

articles/guides/keying-and-arithmetic.ht.title: Keying and arithmetic | Egami
articles/guides/keying-and-arithmetic.ht.summary: Keying and arithmetic Operations that ImageMagick users expect: making a color transparent, replacing a color, flood fill, arithmetic with a constant, and stacking several images. Each matches its ImageMagick option exactly at 8 and 16 bits. Color tolerance Keying compares colors with ImageMagick's -fuzz distance on the stored values: a tolerance from 0 (the exact color) to 1 (every color). Alpha counts three times as much as each color channel, and colors count in proportion to how visible both pixels are, so two fully transparent pixels always match. Make a color transparent // Remove a green screen: within 0.15 of pure green becomes transparent, and alpha ramps back over the next 0.1 for soft edges. photo.Apply(ops => ops.MakeTransparent(new Rgba8(0, 177, 64, 255), tolerance: 0.15f, softness: 0.1f), Ct); MakeTransparent clears alpha where a pixel lies within the tolerance and keeps its color, as ImageMagick's -transparent does. softness ramps alpha back up over the next band of distance, for antialiased edges; with no softness the result is ImageMagick's. Replace a color photo.Apply(ops => ops.ReplaceColor(Rgba8.White, new Rgba8(250, 245, 230, 255), tolerance: 0.05f), Ct); Flood fill // Fill the region around (10, 10) whose colors are close to its own, as a paint bucket does. photo.Apply(ops => ops.FloodFill(new Point(10, 10), Rgba8.White, tolerance: 0.1f), Ct); FloodFill fills the region connected to the seed whose colors lie within the tolerance of the seed's own. It spreads to the four side neighbours by default, as ImageMagick does; Connectivity.Eight adds the diagonals. Its visited set, one bit a pixel, counts against MaxTotalBytes. Inside a scope, the region is found within the scope's area. Select by color // Select by color, then edit only the selection: a magic wand from a point, and every pixel close to a color. using Raster<Gray8> wand = photo.FloodMask(new Point(30, 30), tolerance: 0.12f); using Raster<Gray8> reds = photo.ColorMask(new Rgba8(200, 40, 30, 255), tolerance: 0.2f); photo.Apply(ops => ops .Within(new Mask(wand), o => o.Blur(4)) .Within(new Mask(reds), o => o.Saturation(1.4f)), Ct); ColorMask and FloodMask return a Gray8 mask, 255 inside the selection, for Within(Mask, …). Arithmetic with a constant // Lift the shadows with a log curve, then cap the highlights; values are on a 0 to 1 scale, as ImageMagick's -evaluate. photo.Apply(ops => ops .Arithmetic(PixelMath.Log, 3) .Arithmetic(PixelMath.Min, 0.95f), Ct); Arithmetic applies a PixelMath operator (add, subtract, multiply, divide, pow, log, min, max, set) to the chosen channels, on values scaled 0 to 1 and clamped. 8-bit and 16-bit pixels are evaluated as 16-bit samples and rounded as ImageMagick's Q16 build rounds them, so the result equals -evaluate exactly. Stack images // Average a burst of photos to smooth noise; the median removes things that appear in only a few frames. using Raster mean = Raster.Stack([first, second, third], StackMode.Mean); using Raster clean = Raster.Stack([first, second, third], StackMode.Median); Raster.Stack combines the same channel of the same pixel across two or more rasters (StackMode: mean, median, min, max), as ImageMagick's -evaluate-sequence does for mean, min and max. The median is taken per channel, as Photoshop's median stack does; ImageMagick's picks the whole pixel whose intensity is the median. Stack works a few rows at a time, holding one row of each input.

articles/guides/lighting-and-relief.html.title: Lighting and relief | Egami
articles/guides/lighting-and-relief.html.summary: Lighting and relief Three steps treat an image as a height field and light it. Lighting is the SVG 1.1 lighting filters, with Skia's parameters; Emboss and Shade are the two quick relief effects ImageMagick users know. Operation Does Lighting(light, model, options) SVG's feDiffuseLighting or feSpecularLighting with a distant, point or spot light: returns the light map, or blends it onto the image Emboss(angle, depth, sigma, grayscale) Blurs, takes the slope toward the light, and adds mid gray: flat areas become 0.5 Shade(azimuth, elevation, colored) ImageMagick's -shade (gray relief) or +shade (the shading multiplied onto the colors), identical at 8 bits Lights and surfaces // Three light sources, as SVG and Skia have them. Positions are pixels: x right, y down, z up out of the image. Light sun = new DistantLight(azimuth: 225, elevation: 40); // from the top left, 40° up Light bulb = new PointLight(new Vector3(60, 20, 80)) { Color = new Rgba8(255, 240, 210, 255) }; Light spot = new SpotLight(new Vector3(0, 0, 150), target: new Vector3(120, 60, 0), exponent: 4, coneAngle: 30); // Two ways a surface reflects: matte (N·L) or shiny (a highlight, (N·H)^shininess). LightingModel matte = LightingModel.Diffuse(kd: 1.2f); LightingModel shiny = LightingModel.Specular(ks: 1, shininess: 20); using Raster<Rgba8> map = logo.Derive(ops => ops.Lighting(sun, matte), Ct); // the light map, opaque using Raster<Rgba8> glints = logo.Derive(ops => ops.Lighting(bulb, shiny), Ct); // alpha = brightest channel using Raster<Rgba8> pool = logo.Derive(ops => ops.Lighting(spot, matte), Ct); The height is alpha by default, as in SVG and Skia: a logo on a transparent canvas stands up from it. SurfaceScale is the height of a fully opaque (or white) pixel, in pixels, so larger values give steeper slopes. Normals come from SVG's 3 × 3 Sobel stencils, with SVG's own stencils on the edges and corners of the image. DistantLight(azimuth, elevation) shines from one direction everywhere. The azimuth is SVG's: degrees clockwise from the x axis, with y down, so 225 is the top left. PointLight(position) and SpotLight(position, target, exponent, coneAngle) sit at a point in pixel coordinates, with z above the image; pixel centers are at x + 0.5, as Skia evaluates them. A spot light fades as cos(angle)^exponent away from its axis and stops at the cone angle, with Skia's soft cone edge. LightingModel.Diffuse(kd) gives the light's color times kd times N·L, and an opaque map. LightingModel.Specular(ks, shininess) gives a highlight, ks times (N·H)^shininess, and a map whose alpha is its brightest channel. Light colors and the light map are not color-managed: they work on stored values, as Skia does in its working space. SVG's default of computing filters in linear light is not applied; convert the image first if you need it. // A photo's luminance as the height: light areas stand up. SurfaceScale is the height of white, in pixels. LightingOptions relief = new() { Height = HeightSource.Luminance, SurfaceScale = 6 }; using Raster lit = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Lighting(new DistantLight(300, 50), LightingModel.Diffuse(), relief), Ct); // The same light blended onto the photo instead of replacing it. using Raster shaded = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Lighting(new DistantLight(300, 50), LightingModel.Diffuse(1.3f), relief with { Blend = BlendMode.Overlay }), Ct); A bevelled logo With Blend, the light map is blended onto the image with a 2.5.1 BlendMode, the light map as the source, and the image keeps its alpha, so the light changes the color and never the shape. Multiply shades the slopes away from the light; Screen adds a specular highlight on the slopes that face it. // A logo on a transparent canvas: alpha is the height, so soften its edges first to give them a slope. logo.Apply(ops => ops .Blur(2.5f) .Lighting(new DistantLight(225, 35), LightingModel.Diffuse(1.4f), new LightingOptions { SurfaceScale = 5, Blend = BlendMode.Multiply }) // shade the slopes .Lighting(new DistantLight(225, 35), LightingModel.Specular(0.8f, 24), new LightingOptions { SurfaceScale = 5, Blend = BlendMode.Screen }), Ct); // and add a highlight logo.Save("bevel.png"); Embossed text Emboss turns a page or a photo into gray relief: it blurs with sigma, takes the slope toward the light with a 3 × 3 Sobel stencil, scales it by depth and adds mid gray, so paper becomes flat gray and strokes rise. The angle is counterclockwise from the right with y up, as ImageMagick's -shade azimuth (135 is the top left). grayscale: false embosses each color channel on its own; alpha is kept. // Gray relief: flat paper becomes mid gray, strokes rise toward the light at the top left. using Raster embossed = page.Derive(ops => ops.Emboss(angle: 135, depth: 3, sigma: 1), Ct); // Each color channel on its own, softer and deeper. using Raster colored = page.Derive(ops => ops.Emboss(angle: 45, depth: 6, sigma: 2, grayscale: false), Ct); ImageMagick's -emboss shares only the name: it sharpens along a diagonal and then equalizes the histogram, so its results differ from this classic emboss. Shade Shade is ImageMagick's -shade: the luminance is the height, and each pixel becomes the Lambertian shading by a light at the azimuth (counterclockwise from the right, y up) and elevation; flat areas get sin(elevation). colored: true multiplies the shading onto the colors, as +shade does. Results are identical to ImageMagick 7 (Q16 HDRI) at 8 bits; alpha is kept. // ImageMagick's -shade 30x30 (identical at 8 bits) and +shade 120x45. using Raster gray = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Shade(azimuth: 30, elevation: 30), Ct); using Raster colored = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Shade(azimuth: 120, elevation: 45, colored: true), Ct); Edges and regions All three keep the size and read one pixel past each output (Emboss also the blur's reach), repeating the edge pixel past the border. They work inside Within and OnChannels: inside a region they read the real pixels around it, and a point or spot light keeps its position in the raster's coordinates.

articles/guides/memory-and-threading.htm.title: Memory and threading | Egami
articles/guides/memory-and-threading.htm.summary: Memory and threading The context // Everything that is not specific to one call lives in an immutable EgamiContext. Change it with `with`. EgamiContext context = EgamiContext.Default with { MaxParallelism = 4, // threads one operation may use; 1 is sequential Limits = SafetyLimits.Default with { MaxPixels = 50_000_000 }, }; using Raster image = Raster.Load("duck.png", context); image.Apply(ops => ops.Blur(2)); // uses the raster's context: 4 threads at most A raster remembers the context it was loaded or created with, and its operations use it. EgamiContext.Default serves every call that passes none; EgamiContext.SetDefault replaces it once, at startup, before anything reads it. Threads Operations split the image into bands of rows and run them on up to MaxParallelism threads (the processor count by default). Small images run on one thread, where splitting would cost more than it saves. Decoding is mostly sequential by nature; JPEG splits files at their restart markers, pipelines progressive scans and converts in parallel bands, and animated formats map frames in parallel. PNG compresses large images on several threads when PngWriterOptions.ParallelCompression is set, with the same bytes at any thread count. Rasters are not thread-safe: do not run two chains on the same raster at once. Separate rasters, contexts and loads are independent, and readers, writers and contexts can be shared freely.
