Streaming RasterDecoder decodes a band of rows or a frame at a time, so an image never has to exist whole: // A band of rows at a time: memory is the band plus the format's working set, whatever the image size. using RasterDecoder decoder = RasterDecoder.Open("egret.png"); Console.WriteLine($"{decoder.Info.Width}×{decoder.Info.Height}, {decoder.Info.Access}, holding {decoder.Info.WorkingBytes:N0} bytes"); using Raster<Gray8> band = Raster.Create<Gray8>(decoder.Info.Width, 64); int rows; while ((rows = decoder.ReadRows(band)) > 0) { for (int y = 0; y < rows; y++) { foreach (Gray8 pixel in band.Row(y)) { sum += pixel.L; } } } ReaderOptions.Region decodes only a rectangle and MinimumSize a reduced size, in Load, Probe and the decoder alike. RasterInfo.Access says whether a format streams its rows (RasterAccess.Streamed) or is decoded into a buffer first (RasterAccess.Buffered), and WorkingBytes how much the decode holds besides your band: // Only a rectangle, at a quarter of its size or a little more. ReaderOptions options = new() { Region = new Rect(100, 200, 256, 256), MinimumSize = new Size(64, 64) }; RasterInfo info = Raster.Probe("egret.png", options: options); // Access and WorkingBytes before decoding using Raster tile = Raster.Load("egret.png", options: options); Raster.LoadInto decodes into a raster you already have, and ReadFrame gives an animation one composed frame at a time: // Decode into a raster you already have: video frames and pooled images reuse their memory. using Raster<Rgb8> reused = Raster.Create<Rgb8>(480, 640); Raster.LoadInto("egret.png", reused); // An animation one composed frame at a time, into one reused canvas. using RasterDecoder gif = RasterDecoder.Open("pan.gif"); using Raster<Rgba8> canvas = Raster.Create<Rgba8>(gif.Info.Width, gif.Info.Height); while (gif.ReadFrame(canvas) is Metadata.FrameMetadata frame) { Console.WriteLine($"frame {count++}, shown for {frame.Delay.TotalMilliseconds} ms"); } RasterDecoder.OpenIncremental decodes while the bytes are still arriving: Append each chunk as it comes, read the rows finished so far, and call EndOfInput after the last. Status (a DecodeStatus) says whether rows are ready, more bytes are needed, or the frame or image is done, and RenderPreview draws an interlaced PNG, a progressive JPEG or a GIF frame as far as it has arrived. Files that are decoded into a buffer first (such as bottom-up BMP and TGA) wait for the end. // Decode while the bytes arrive, a chunk at a time, as from a download. using RasterDecoder decoder = RasterDecoder.OpenIncremental(); Raster<Rgb8>? band = null; foreach (ReadOnlyMemory<byte> chunk in file.Chunk(4096).Select(c => new ReadOnlyMemory<byte>(c))) { decoder.Append(chunk.Span); if (decoder.HeaderRead) { band ??= Raster.Create<Rgb8>(decoder.Info.Width, 16); int rows; while ((rows = decoder.ReadRows(band)) > 0) { rowsSoFar += rows; // the rows finished so far; an interlaced file shows RenderPreview instead } } } decoder.EndOfInput(); while (decoder.ReadRows(band!) is int rest and > 0) { rowsSoFar += rest; } band?.Dispose(); On a server, RasterDecoder.OpenAsync reads an asynchronous stream the same way, and LoadAsync from a stream that cannot seek, such as a request body, no longer holds the whole file while it decodes: // On a server: read rows as the upload arrives, without holding the whole file. await using Stream upload = File.OpenRead("egret.png"); using RasterDecoder decoder = await RasterDecoder.OpenAsync(upload, cancellationToken: TestContext.Current.CancellationToken); using Raster<Gray8> band = Raster.Create<Gray8>(decoder.Info.Width, 32); int rows; while ((rows = await decoder.ReadRowsAsync(band, TestContext.Current.CancellationToken)) > 0) { for (int y = 0; y < rows; y++) { sum += band.Row(y)[0].L; } } RasterEncoder writes the other way: a band of rows or a frame at a time, into a file or stream, with the bytes Save writes. Options that need every pixel before the first byte, such as an automatic palette, PNG's Reduce or choosing alpha by looking at the pixels, throw NotSupportedException at Create and say what to set instead. BMP and TGA store rows bottom-up: on a stream that cannot seek they are written top-down, as is run-length TGA, and an APNG there needs PngWriterOptions.FrameCount. An interlaced PNG (PngWriterOptions.Interlace) holds the rows until the last one, since its first pass needs the whole height. // A huge image written a band at a time: only the band is ever in memory. const int Width = 8_000, Height = 6_000; using Raster<Rgb8> band = Raster.Create<Rgb8>(Width, 64); using RasterEncoder<Rgb8> encoder = RasterEncoder.Create<Rgb8>("big.png", Width, Height); for (int top = 0; top < Height; top += band.Height) { int rows = Math.Min(band.Height, Height - top); for (int y = 0; y < rows; y++) { band.Row(y).Fill(new Rgb8((byte)(top + y), 128, 200)); } encoder.WriteRows(band, rows); } encoder.Complete(); // writes IEND; without it the file is deleted on dispose // An animation written a frame at a time, each frame from one reused canvas. using Raster<Rgba8> canvas = Raster.Create<Rgba8>(120, 80); using FileStream file = File.Create("spinner.gif"); using RasterEncoder<Rgba8> gif = RasterEncoder.Create<Rgba8>(file, GifFormat.Info, 120, 80); for (int i = 0; i < 12; i++) { for (int y = 0; y < canvas.Height; y++) { canvas.Row(y).Fill(new Rgba8(255, 255, 255, 255)); } canvas.Row(40)[(i * 10)..((i * 10) + 10)].Fill(new Rgba8(200, 0, 0, 255)); gif.WriteFrame(canvas, new Metadata.FrameMetadata { Delay = TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(80) }); } gif.Complete(); WriteRowsAsync and CompleteAsync write each band out asynchronously, and SaveAsync now does the same instead of encoding the whole file into memory first: // On a server: send each band as it is encoded, without holding the file. using RasterDecoder source = RasterDecoder.Open("egret.png"); using Raster<Rgb8> band = Raster.Create<Rgb8>(source.Info.Width, 32); using RasterEncoder<Rgb8> encoder = RasterEncoder.Create<Rgb8>(response, JpegFormat.Info, source.Info.Width, source.Info.Height); int rows; while ((rows = source.ReadRows(band)) > 0) { await encoder.WriteRowsAsync(band, rows, TestContext.Current.CancellationToken); } await encoder.CompleteAsync(TestContext.Current.CancellationToken); Raster.Transcode joins the two: rows go from the decoder through a short chain of operations into the encoder, so a thumbnail of a 20,000 × 20,000 PNG holds well under a megabyte of pixels instead of 1.6 GB. When the chain starts with Fit, Cover or Resize, the decoder already shrinks by a whole factor (MinimumSize), and a leading Crop becomes Region. The chain may crop, resize, mirror left to right and adjust colors pixel by pixel; anything that needs rows out of order or the whole image, such as Blur or Rotate, throws NotSupportedException before anything is written. // A thumbnail of a big file without ever holding the full image: the decoder already shrinks by a whole factor. Raster.Transcode("egret.png", "thumb.jpg", x => x.Fit(256, 256).Saturation(1.1f)); // On a server: an upload to a 512-pixel PNG preview, streamed both ways. await using Stream upload = File.OpenRead("egret.png"); await Raster.TranscodeAsync(upload, response, PngFormat.Info, x => x.Fit(512, 512), cancellationToken: TestContext.Current.CancellationToken); Pixel memory Pixel memory never lives on the garbage-collected heap as large arrays. PooledPixelMemorySource.Shared hands out pooled arrays for small blocks and 64-byte-aligned unmanaged memory for large ones, keeps up to 128 MB of freed blocks for reuse, and splits very large images into blocks of whole rows. Trim() frees what it keeps. You can plug in your own source through EgamiContext.Memory by implementing IPixelMemorySource. Finding leaks PixelMemoryUsage usage = PooledPixelMemorySource.Shared.Usage; Console.WriteLine($"{usage.LiveBlocks} blocks, {usage.LiveBytes:N0} bytes in use"); // Looking for a raster someone forgot to dispose: track leaks for a while, with stack traces. usage.CaptureStackTraces = true; usage.LeakDetected += (_, leak) => Console.WriteLine($"{leak.Bytes:N0} bytes never disposed, allocated at\n{leak.StackTrace}"); usage.TrackLeaks = true; LiveBlocks and LiveBytes are always counted, at the cost of one atomic addition per allocation. TrackLeaks gives each new block a small finalizable tracker, so turn it on only while you look; CaptureStackTraces makes allocations much slower still. LeakDetected runs on the finalizer thread. Leaks come only through LeakDetected, never through the diagnostics handler, which reports what one call found. Your own memory source // Every pixel buffer comes from the context's IPixelMemorySource; wrap the pooled one to count what it hands out. CountingSource counting = new(PooledPixelMemorySource.Shared); EgamiContext context = EgamiContext.Default with { Memory = counting }; using (Raster<Rgba8> image = Raster.Create<Rgba8>(512, 512, context)) { image.Apply(ops => ops.Blur(2)); } Console.WriteLine($"{counting.Blocks} blocks, {counting.Bytes:N0} bytes"); private sealed class CountingSource(IPixelMemorySource inner) : IPixelMemorySource { public int Blocks; public long Bytes; public int MaxBlockBytes => inner.MaxBlockBytes; public IMemoryOwner<byte> Allocate(int byteLength, ClearMode clear) { Interlocked.Increment(ref Blocks); Interlocked.Add(ref Bytes, byteLength); return inner.Allocate(byteLength, clear); // ClearMode.Zero when the caller needs zeroed memory } } // In tests or debug builds: report a raster that was never disposed, and where it was allocated. PooledPixelMemorySource memory = new(); memory.Usage.TrackLeaks = true; memory.Usage.CaptureStackTraces = true; memory.Usage.LeakDetected += (sender, e) => Console.Error.WriteLine($"Leaked {e.Bytes:N0} bytes, allocated at:\n{e.StackTrace}"); Run it samples/MemoryAndThreading is a console app that does what this guide shows on the bundled images: dotnet run --project samples/MemoryAndThreading writes its results to ./output.

articles/guides/metadata.html.title: Metadata | Egami
articles/guides/metadata.html.summary: Metadata raster.Metadata holds what a file says beside its pixels. It is kept apart from the pixels, survives operations unless an operation makes it wrong, and is written back by every format that can carry it. Item Read from Written to Exif (ExifData) JPEG, PNG (eXIf, and the legacy "Raw profile type" chunks) JPEG, PNG Iptc (IptcData) JPEG (APP13), PNG ("Raw profile type iptc") JPEG, PNG Xmp, XmpData JPEG (with extended XMP), PNG, GIF JPEG, PNG, GIF IccProfile JPEG, PNG, GIF, BMP (V5) JPEG, PNG, GIF, BMP Text PNG text chunks, GIF comments, PNM comments, TGA author and comments The same Resolution PNG, JPEG, BMP PNG, JPEG, BMP ColorSpace, Gamma PNG, QOI, TGA PNG, QOI LoopCount, frame Delay GIF, APNG GIF, APNG FormatDetails Every format: what only it has The same format, for round trips Warnings Every reader: what a lenient read recovered from Never RasterMetadata metadata = image.Metadata; metadata.Text.Add(new TextEntry("Comment", "Made with Egami")); metadata.Resolution = new Resolution(300, 300, ResolutionUnit.PerInch); Console.WriteLine($"{metadata.ColorSpace}, ICC {metadata.IccProfile.Length} bytes, XMP {metadata.Xmp.Length} bytes"); foreach (EgamiDiagnostic warning in metadata.Warnings) { Console.WriteLine($"Recovered from: {warning.Message} ({warning.Id})"); } image.Save("duck-300dpi.png"); EXIF if (image.Metadata.Exif is ExifData exif) { Console.WriteLine($"{exif.CameraMake} {exif.CameraModel}, {exif.DateTaken}, {exif.Location}"); if (exif.TryGet(ExifKey.ExposureTime, out ExifEntry? exposure)) { Console.WriteLine($"1/{1 / exposure.AsDouble():0} s"); } exif.Set(ExifKey.Copyright, "© 2026 Example"); exif.Remove(ExifKey.GpsLatitude); } Common values have typed properties (Orientation, DateTaken, CameraMake, CameraModel, Location); any tag can be read with TryGet and written with Set. A block you do not edit is saved back byte for byte; an edited one is laid out again, in tag order. A damaged block keeps its raw bytes and sets IsDamaged, and the pixels still load. ExifData.Parse reads a block on its own, capped by SafetyLimits.MaxMetadataBytes. What operations do to metadata Rotating, flipping and AutoOrient set the EXIF orientation to Normal and drop the embedded thumbnail, which would otherwise show sideways. Resizing and cropping, including your own operations that change the size, update the EXIF pixel dimensions and drop the embedded thumbnail, which no longer matches. Every geometry operation moves the EXIF SubjectArea and SubjectLocation with the picture: shifted by crops and pads, scaled by resizes, mirrored and turned with flips and rotations, clipped to a crop and dropped when the subject leaves it. Their XMP copies, and the XMP tiff:Orientation, exif:PixelXDimension and exif:PixelYDimension, follow the same rules. A tag the file does not have is never added. Color operations change nothing in the metadata. Removing metadata // Every writer's options have StripMetadata: the pixels are written, EXIF, XMP, ICC and text are not. image.Save("clean.jpg", new JpegWriterOptions { StripMetadata = true }); Typed EXIF values using Raster photo = Raster.Load("sideways.jpg"); ExifData exif = photo.Metadata.Exif ?? new ExifData(); // Typed values go in with their EXIF type; fractions are exact numerator / denominator pairs. exif.Set(ExifKey.ExposureTime, new ExifFraction(1, 250)); exif.Set(ExifKey.Artist, "A. Photographer"); if (exif.TryGet(ExifKey.ExposureTime, out ExifEntry? entry) && entry.Type == ExifType.Rational) { Console.WriteLine($"Exposure {entry.AsFraction()} s = {entry.AsFraction().ToDouble()} s, in the {entry.Key.Ifd} IFD"); } if (exif.Location is GeoPosition where) { Console.WriteLine($"Taken at {where.Latitude:F5}, {where.Longitude:F5}"); } The IFD1 thumbnail decodes as a raster, and a new one is made from any raster. Crops, resizes, flips and turns drop the thumbnail, since it no longer shows the image: using Raster photo = Raster.Load("sideways.jpg"); // The thumbnail as stored, if the file has one; ReadThumbnail returns null otherwise. using (Raster<Rgb8>? stored = photo.Metadata.Exif?.ReadThumbnail()) { Console.WriteLine(stored is null ? "No thumbnail" : $"Thumbnail {stored.Width} x {stored.Height}"); } // Turning the image drops the thumbnail, which would show sideways; make a new one from the result. photo.Apply(ops => ops.AutoOrient()); photo.Metadata.Exif?.SetThumbnail(photo); photo.Save("upright.jpg"); The Windows XP tags (ExifKey.XPTitle, XPComment, XPAuthor, XPKeywords, XPSubject) and the encoded strings (ExifKey.UserComment, GpsProcessingMethod, GpsAreaInformation) read and write as text through ExifEntry.AsString and ExifData.Set, in the encodings Windows Explorer and cameras use. EXIF stored somewhere else, such as a database, parses on its own: // EXIF from somewhere other than an image file (a database column, a sidecar), with a cap on the bytes of values read. ExifData exif = ExifData.Parse(tiff.Span, SafetyLimits.Default with { MaxMetadataBytes = 64 * 1024 }); foreach (string warning in exif.Warnings) { Console.WriteLine($"EXIF: {warning}"); } IPTC IptcData holds IPTC-IIM datasets, as news agencies, stock libraries and Lightroom write them. Each IptcEntry has an IptcKey (record and dataset, such as 2:25 for keywords), and typed getters cover the common ones. Values longer than the IIM specification allows are refused on Set and Add; long text belongs in XMP. Text that is not ASCII switches the block to UTF-8. using Raster photo = Raster.Load("sideways.jpg"); IptcData iptc = photo.Metadata.Iptc ?? new IptcData(); iptc.Headline = "Harbour at dawn"; iptc.Keywords = [.. iptc.Keywords, "harbour", "Bergen"]; // Any dataset by its key; Add appends to the repeatable ones. iptc.Set(IptcKey.City, "Bergen"); // Text that is not ASCII sets the coded character set (1:90) to UTF-8, so other programs read it right. iptc.Caption = "Fishing boats at Bryggen, Bergen — first light"; foreach (IptcEntry entry in iptc.Entries) { Console.WriteLine($"{entry.Key} {entry.AsString()}"); } // JPEG saves it in its Photoshop resource block (APP13), with the digest Photoshop and Lightroom check. photo.Metadata.Iptc = iptc; photo.Save("captioned.jpg"); IPTC stored somewhere else parses on its own: // IPTC datasets from somewhere other than an image file, with a cap on the bytes of values read. IptcData iptc = IptcData.Parse(iim.Span, SafetyLimits.Default with { MaxMetadataBytes = 64 * 1024 }); Console.WriteLine($"{iptc.Get(IptcKey.ObjectName)}: {iptc.Entries.Count} datasets, damaged: {iptc.IsDamaged}"); XMP XmpData is a parsed XMP packet. Properties are addressed by XmpName (a namespace URI from XmpNamespaces and a local name), never by prefix. A property is a simple value, an XmpArray (bag, sequence or language alternatives, an XmpArrayKind) or an XmpStruct; typed properties cover the Dublin Core, XMP Basic, Photoshop and TIFF values apps use most. An edited packet is written as canonical RDF/XML with padding; properties Egami does not know are kept. XmpData xmp = new() { Title = "Harbour at dawn", Creators = ["A. Photographer"], Keywords = ["harbour", "Bergen"], Rating = 4, }; // Any property, by namespace URI and local name; structures and arrays nest. XmpStruct contact = new(); contact.Set(new XmpName(XmpNamespaces.IptcCore, "CiEmailWork"), "photo@example.com"); xmp.Set(new XmpName(XmpNamespaces.IptcCore, "CreatorContactInfo"), contact); if (xmp.TryGet(new XmpName(XmpNamespaces.DublinCore, "title"), out object? title) && title is XmpArray languages) { languages.SetLanguage("nb-NO", "Havn ved daggry"); } ReadOnlyMemory<byte> packet = xmp.ToBytes(); // canonical RDF/XML with padding RasterMetadata.XmpData is a live view of RasterMetadata.Xmp: it parses the packet on first use, and once edited, the edit is the packet every format saves. JPEG, PNG (an iTXt chunk) and GIF carry XMP. using Raster photo = Raster.Load("sideways.jpg"); // The parsed view of the packet; it is null when the file has none, so start one. XmpData xmp = photo.Metadata.XmpData ??= new XmpData(); xmp.Keywords = [.. xmp.Keywords, "harbour"]; xmp.Rating = 5; // The edit is the packet now: Metadata.Xmp returns it and every format saves it. photo.Save("rated.png"); // An XMP packet from a sidecar file or a database; DTDs are refused and nothing outside it is read. XmpData xmp = XmpData.Parse(packet.Span, SafetyLimits.Default with { MaxMetadataBytes = 1024 * 1024 }); Console.WriteLine(xmp.IsDamaged ? string.Join(" ", xmp.Warnings) : $"Label: {xmp.Label}"); Color space RasterMetadata.ColorSpace says what the file declared about its colors. Egami keeps the declaration and the profile bytes; it does not convert between color spaces. using Raster image = Raster.Load("duck.png"); string note = image.Metadata.ColorSpace switch { ColorSpaceHint.Srgb or ColorSpaceHint.Unknown => "sRGB: shown as is", ColorSpaceHint.Linear => "linear light: encode before showing", ColorSpaceHint.Gamma => "a file gamma other than sRGB", ColorSpaceHint.EmbeddedIcc => "an ICC profile describes the colors", _ => "unknown", }; Run it samples/Metadata is a console app that does what this guide shows on the bundled images: dotnet run --project samples/Metadata writes its results to ./output.

articles/guides/metafiles.html.title: Windows metafiles | Egami
articles/guides/metafiles.html.summary: Windows metafiles Egami.Metafiles plays Windows metafiles, the vector pictures Office and Windows programs exchange: WMF (Windows Metafile), EMF (Enhanced Metafile) and EMF+ (GDI+ records inside an EMF), and their gzip forms WMZ and EMZ. It draws them through Egami.Drawing's canvas, so a chart pasted from Excel stays vector on a PDF page or in SVG output and rasterizes the same on any OS. It only reads and plays: it does not write metafiles. It is fully managed. Loading Metafile.Load reads a file, a stream or bytes in memory; gzip is detected by its first bytes. Metafile.Kind says what it holds (a MetafileKind: Wmf, Emf, EmfPlusDual or EmfPlusOnly), and the header gives the picture's size: Size and Frame are in points: an EMF's frame rectangle (0.01 mm), a placeable WMF's box and units per inch, or, for a WMF without a placeable header, its window extent at 96 DPI (with a Metafile.NoPlaceableHeader warning). Dpi is the resolution the records were made at, and Description an EMF's application and picture names. Loading is lenient: a record that runs past the end of the file ends the walk with a warning, and what came before it plays. Warnings lists what the load found; MetafileLoadOptions.Context sets the limits (the file size and what EMZ and WMZ inflate to) and the diagnostics handler. // Untrusted files: the context's limits bound the file size and what EMZ and WMZ inflate to; a record that runs past // the end is skipped with a warning, and what came before it plays. MetafileLoadOptions options = new() { Context = EgamiContext.Default with { Limits = SafetyLimits.Default with { MaxTotalBytes = 16 << 20 } }, }; Metafile picture = Metafile.Load(new MemoryStream(bytes), options); if (picture.Kind is MetafileKind.EmfPlusDual or MetafileKind.EmfPlusOnly) { Console.WriteLine("Drawn by its EMF+ records, as GDI+ draws it."); } A picture taken out of a document is often already in memory; Load takes the bytes as they are. // A picture taken out of a document, already in memory: no stream needed. Metafile picture = Metafile.Load(bytes); using Raster<Rgba8> page = Raster.Create<Rgba8>(200, 150); using RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = page.CreateCanvas(); picture.Draw(canvas, new RectF(0, 0, 200, 150)); Drawing Metafile.Draw plays the picture on any canvas: in points from the canvas's origin, or with its frame stretched to a box, as Word stretches a picture to its frame. Metafile.Rasterize draws into a new raster at a DPI (96 by default) or a width and height, over a background: // WMF, EMF and EMF+ alike, and the gzip forms WMZ and EMZ. Metafile chart = Metafile.Load(path); Console.WriteLine($"{chart.Kind}, {chart.Size.X} by {chart.Size.Y} points"); // At twice the screen's resolution, over white; text uses the installed fonts. using Raster<Rgba8> image = chart.Rasterize<Rgba8>(new MetafileRenderOptions { Dpi = 192, Background = new RgbaF32(1, 1, 1, 1), }); image.Save(output); Metafile picture = Metafile.Load(path); // The frame is stretched to the box, as Word stretches a picture to its frame. The same calls draw on a PDF page. using Raster<Rgba8> page = Raster.Create<Rgba8>(400, 300); using RasterCanvas<Rgba8> canvas = page.CreateCanvas(); canvas.Clear(new RgbaF32(1, 1, 1, 1)); picture.Draw(canvas, new RectF(50, 50, 300, 200)); MetafileRenderOptions carries the rest: Antialias is on by default; off, GDI records draw aliased as GDI itself draws them, which is what to compare with Windows. EMF+ records follow the file's own smoothing either way. Playback (a MetafilePlayback) picks which records of a dual file play: Auto, the EMF+ records as GDI+ plays them, or Gdi, the GDI records only, as programs without GDI+ draw the file. Fonts and FontSubstitutions choose the faces for text; TextAsPaths draws text as outlines. // A dual EMF+ file plays its EMF+ records by default, as Office and GDI+ do; Gdi plays only the GDI records, as // programs without GDI+ draw it. Metafile picture = Metafile.Load(path); using Raster<Rgba8> gdi = picture.Rasterize<Rgba8>(new MetafileRenderOptions { Playback = MetafilePlayback.Gdi }); Text and fonts Text records name a face, and each glyph's place comes from the record itself, so a line keeps its length in another face. A face the fonts lack is replaced by a metric-compatible open font where one exists (Arial by Liberation Sans or Arimo, Times New Roman by Liberation Serif or Tinos, Courier New by Liberation Mono or Cousine, Calibri by Carlito, Cambria by Caladea), then by your FontSubstitutions, then by the generic family; each substitution is a Metafile.FontSubstituted warning. Symbol and Wingdings text maps to Unicode in a substitute. Text given as glyph indices (Word writes these for complex scripts) is drawn only in the face it was made for, since another face would show the wrong letters. // Faces the machine lacks: the built-in table maps Calibri to Carlito, Arial to Liberation Sans and so on; add your own. Metafile picture = Metafile.Load(path); using Raster<Rgba8> image = picture.Rasterize<Rgba8>(new MetafileRenderOptions { FontSubstitutions = new Dictionary<string, string> { ["Segoe UI"] = "Noto Sans" }, Antialias = false, // GDI's own aliased look, for comparing with Windows }); Raster.Load Registered with EgamiContext.WithFormat, MetafileFormat lets Raster.Load draw a metafile at its size at 96 DPI onto a transparent Rgba8 raster, and Raster.Probe give that size from the header without drawing. MetafileDecodeOptions.Dpi sets another resolution. // Register the format once; Raster.Load then draws metafiles at their own size at 96 DPI. EgamiContext context = EgamiContext.Default.WithFormat(MetafileFormat.Info); using Raster raster = Raster.Load(path, context); RasterInfo info = Raster.Probe(path, context); // the size from the header, nothing drawn // MetafileDecodeOptions sets the resolution; Raster.Load then draws at that DPI. using Raster sharp = Raster.Load(path, context, new MetafileDecodeOptions { Dpi = 300 }); What plays, and how close it is The GDI records of WMF and EMF play as GDI plays them: map modes, the world transform, pens and brushes (hatches and pattern brushes sized from the reference device, so they scale with the picture), paths, clipping regions, bitmaps through Egami's BMP reader, and text. Drawn aliased, the synthetic test files match Windows GDI within a mean of one level and 99% of pixels within 16 levels, family by family; text is measured with a looser bound, since GDI hints glyphs to whole pixels. Raster operations Egami draws with the nearest blend: AND as multiply, OR as lighten, XOR as difference, and the common transparent-bitmap idioms as one masked image; others draw as a copy with a Metafile.RasterOperation warning. EMF+ records play as GDI+ plays them: the world and page transforms, containers, clips with all six combine modes, smoothing, pixel offset and compositing; solid, hatch, texture, linear and path gradient brushes (path gradients as a Gouraud mesh); pens with dashes, compound lines, inset alignment and anchor and arrow caps; cardinal curves; images, with JPEG and PNG handed to the canvas unchanged so a PDF page embeds them as they are, and metafile images played as vectors up to eight levels deep; GDI+ 1.1 image effects; DrawString laid out in its rectangle and DrawDriverString. In a dual file the GDI records play only where GDI+ hands drawing to GDI (EmfPlusGetDC). Flood fills, OpenGL records, escapes and PostScript carried in comments are skipped with a Metafile.SkippedRecord warning. The diagnostics page lists every Metafile.* id.

articles/guides/palettes.html.title: Palettes and dithering | Egami
articles/guides/palettes.html.summary: Palettes and dithering The palette machinery behind the GIF, palette PNG, BMP and TGA writers, opened up: build a palette or bring your own, reduce an image to it in its own pixel type, get the indices, and pick from the published dithers. Types live in Egami.Quantization. Reduce colors // A 16-color poster with Atkinson's dither; the pixel type stays as it was. photo.Apply(ops => ops.Quantize(new PaletteOptions { MaxColors = 16, Dither = DitherMode.Atkinson }), Ct); photo.Save("poster.png"); RasterOps.Quantize gives each frame a palette (its own colors when they fit, Wu's quantizer otherwise) and replaces each pixel by its palette color, keeping the pixel type: an Rgba16 image stays Rgba16 with at most MaxColors distinct values. The PaletteOptions that the writers take drive it: MaxColors, Dither and AlphaThreshold, as in 1.0. FixedPalette: a fixed palette instead of building one. Every writer that takes PaletteOptions honours it, and throws, naming both numbers, when it has more colors than the format allows. DitherStrength, 0 to 1: how much of the error is diffused, or how tall the ordered pattern is. Serpentine: error diffusion alternates direction from row to row. RefineIterations: k-means passes (Lloyd's algorithm on every fourth pixel) that polish Wu's palette; they never make it fit worse. ExactMatching: each color goes to its exact nearest palette color rather than through the 64-level lookup table. Kernel: a custom ErrorDiffusionKernel instead of Dither. The defaults are 1.0's: Wu's palette, Floyd–Steinberg at full strength, left to right, table matching. Every GIF, PNG, BMP and TGA file Egami wrote before stays the same byte for byte. Dithers DitherMode has 1.0's FloydSteinberg, Ordered (8 × 8 Bayer) and None, plus Atkinson, Burkes, Jarvis–Judice–Ninke, Sierra (three rows, two rows and Lite), Stevenson–Arce and Stucki error diffusion with their published kernels; Riemersma, error diffusion along a Hilbert curve; and Bayer2x2, Bayer4x4, Bayer16x16 and Ordered3x3 patterns. Error diffusion runs row after row; ordered patterns treat every pixel alike, so animation frames dither the same way. Posterize takes the same modes. // A custom error-diffusion kernel: half the error to the right, a quarter down and a quarter down-left, at 80% strength, // scanning every other row backwards. ErrorDiffusionKernel kernel = new(new[,] { { 0, 0, 2 }, { 1, 1, 0 } }, divisor: 4, origin: 1); photo.Apply(ops => ops.Quantize(new PaletteOptions { MaxColors = 8, Kernel = kernel, DitherStrength = 0.8f, Serpentine = true }), Ct); Fixed palettes // Map onto a fixed palette: here an e-ink display's six inks. Palette inks = Palette.FromColors([Rgba8.Black, Rgba8.White, new(255, 0, 0, 255), new(255, 255, 0, 255), new(0, 0, 255, 255), new(0, 255, 0, 255)]); photo.Apply(ops => ops.Remap(inks, DitherMode.FloydSteinberg), Ct); Palette.FromColors takes up to 256 colors and an optional transparent entry. RasterOps.Remap maps onto a palette as ImageMagick's -remap does, keeping each pixel's alpha when the palette is opaque. Palette.Build and Palette.FromRaster build one from every frame of an image; Nearest and NearestIndex look colors up. // Build one palette from an image, polished by k-means, and use it for other images and for every GIF frame. Palette shared = Palette.Build(first, new PaletteOptions { MaxColors = 64, RefineIterations = 6 }); second.Apply(ops => ops.Remap(shared), Ct); second.Save("egret.gif", new GifWriterOptions { Palette = new PaletteOptions { FixedPalette = shared, Dither = DitherMode.Bayer4x4 } }); Palettes has ready-made ones: // Ready-made palettes: web-safe colors, black and white, gray levels, and color cubes such as 3-3-2. using Raster web = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Remap(Quantization.Palettes.WebSafe, DitherMode.Ordered), Ct); using Raster bilevel = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Remap(Quantization.Palettes.BlackAndWhite, DitherMode.Riemersma), Ct); using Raster fourGrays = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Remap(Quantization.Palettes.Grayscale(4)), Ct); using Raster rgb332 = photo.Derive(ops => ops.Remap(Quantization.Palettes.Uniform(8, 8, 4), DitherMode.Bayer16x16), Ct); Indices // Indices plus palette, for a PDF indexed-color image or a format of your own. using IndexedImage indexed = photo.ToIndexed(new PaletteOptions { MaxColors = 64 }); byte[] lookup = [.. indexed.Palette.Colors.SelectMany(c => new[] { c.R, c.G, c.B })]; byte[] samples = indexed.Indices.ToArray(); Raster.ToIndexed returns an IndexedImage: a byte per pixel and the palette, as a palette PNG would store them. The indices are pooled, so dispose it. Dominant colors // The main colors and how much of the picture each covers, e.g. to pick brand colors from a logo or a placeholder color. IReadOnlyList<WeightedColor> colors = logo.DominantColors(5); foreach ((Rgba8 color, double weight) in colors) { Console.WriteLine($"#{color.R:X2}{color.G:X2}{color.B:X2} covers {weight:P0}"); } Raster.DominantColors returns WeightedColors, largest share first. The image is averaged down to at most DominantColorOptions.MaxSamples pixels, transparent ones left out, and clustered by k-means in Oklab, seeded by Wu's palette so the result is the same on every run; clusters closer than MergeDistance merge. The weights of the colors returned sum to 1.

articles/guides/paragraph-layout.html.title: Paragraph layout | Egami
articles/guides/paragraph-layout.html.summary: Paragraph layout Egami.Fonts lays out paragraphs in the Egami.Fonts.Layout namespace: it finds where lines may break (UAX #14), turns styled text into shaped runs with the shaper from Unicode text and shaping, and builds lines at a width, with alignment and justification, line height, spacing, tabs, max lines and ellipsis, inline placeholders, vertical lines, decorations and shadows, and carets and selection for editors. The result is plain geometry (lines of GlyphRuns and decoration shapes), so Egami.Drawing's canvas, a PDF canvas and SVG draw it the same way. Line breaking LineBreaks.Enumerate walks a text's break opportunities through a LineBreakEnumerator that allocates nothing. Each LineBreak gives the index the next line would start at, whether the line must end there (after a newline, CR LF, NEL, VT, FF, U+2028 or U+2029) and whether the break follows a soft hyphen (U+00AD), which shows a hyphen when a line ends there. The last break is always at the end of the text. // Where lines may end: after spaces and hyphens, and always at the end; a line must end after a newline. List<int> breaks = []; foreach (LineBreak b in LineBreaks.Enumerate("A well-known fact.\nNext")) { breaks.Add(b.Index); // 2, 7, 13, 19 (mandatory), 23 } // CSS switches: break-all lets letters break like ideographs. LineBreakOptions breakAll = new(WordBreak: WordBreak.BreakAll); int count = 0; foreach (LineBreak b in LineBreaks.Enumerate("word", breakAll)) { count++; // 4: after every letter } The rules are Unicode's line breaking algorithm (UAX #14) from Egami's own Unicode 17.0 tables, with each character's LineBreakClass from UnicodeData.GetLineBreakClass. LineBreakOptions adds CSS Text 3's switches: WordBreak.BreakAll lets letters and digits of any script break like ideographs; WordBreak.KeepAll keeps ideographs, kana and Hangul together like the letters of a word, for Korean text with spaces. LineBreakStrictness sets how Chinese and Japanese text breaks. Auto is CSS's default and the same as Normal: a line may start with a small kana, and in Chinese and Japanese (Language "zh" or "ja") with the hyphens U+2010, U+2013, U+301C and U+30A0. Loose also lets iteration marks, centred punctuation, wide prefixes and suffixes and inseparable characters break in Chinese and Japanese. Strict is UAX #14's own rules, which pass Unicode's LineBreakTest.txt in full. Anywhere breaks between any two grapheme clusters. OverflowWrap says whether a piece too wide for its line may break between grapheme clusters; line filling uses it. Thai, Lao, Khmer and Myanmar text breaks only at spaces and zero width spaces: Egami has no dictionaries. An object replacement character (U+FFFC, as placeholders use) breaks before and after. Rich text and paragraphs A RichText is a string with StyleSpans over it (start and length in UTF-16 units, never overlapping) and a Placeholder for each object replacement character (U+FFFC). RichTextBuilder builds one: Push a TextStyle, Append text, AddPlaceholder for an inline box, Pop back. Pushed styles nest, and the result has one flat span per stretch of equal style. // Font families come from a collection; later families cover what the first lacks. FontCollection fonts = new(); fonts.AddFile(System.IO.Path.Combine(folder, "NotoSans-Regular.ttf")); fonts.AddFile(System.IO.Path.Combine(folder, "NotoSansArabic-Regular.ttf")); fonts.TryGetFamily("Noto Sans", out FontFamily latin); fonts.TryGetFamily("Noto Sans Arabic", out FontFamily arabic); // Styles nest: the inner span keeps the outer one's size and adds a color and an underline. RichText text = new RichTextBuilder() .Append("Peace is ") .Push(new TextStyle { Size = 20 }) .Append("\u0633\u0644\u0627\u0645 ") .Push(new TextStyle { Color = new Rgba8(200, 30, 30, 255), Decoration = new TextDecoration() }) .Append("in Arabic") .Pop() .Pop() .AddPlaceholder(new Placeholder(16, 16, PlaceholderAlignment.Middle)) .ToRichText(); ParagraphStyle style = new() { DefaultStyle = new TextStyle { FontFamilies = [latin, arabic], Size = 16, LineHeight = LineHeight.Multiple(1.4f) }, Align = TextAlign.Justify, LineBreaking = new LineBreakOptions(WordBreak: WordBreak.Normal), }; // Shaped once: lay it out at any width later. Paragraph paragraph = Paragraph.Create(text, style); Every TextStyle field is optional. An unset field takes the enclosing builder style's, then the ParagraphStyle's DefaultStyle, then Egami's default (16 units, black, normal line height): Fonts: FontFamilies in order of preference (later families and the paragraph's Fallback cover what the first lacks, per grapheme cluster), Size, FontStyle, Variations, Language and OpenType Features. Paint: Color (an Rgba8), or a Paint, which is any ITextPaint; Egami.Drawing's Paint is one, so gradients and image paints reach text. Background or BackgroundPaint fill behind the text, Decoration adds a TextDecoration (its TextDecorationLines, TextDecorationStyle and TextDecorationSkipInk), and Shadows a list of TextShadows. Spacing: LetterSpacing after each grapheme cluster (which turns optional ligatures off), WordSpacing, a LineHeight (Normal, a Multiple of the font size or an Absolute height, by its LineHeightKind) and a BaselineShift. A Placeholder has a width, a height and a PlaceholderAlignment: on the baseline at a given offset, above or below it, or at the line box's top, bottom or middle. Bidi, line breaking and indexes treat it as one character. ParagraphStyle holds the rest: the DefaultStyle, the paragraph Direction, TextAlign, TextAlignLast and TextJustify, the LineBreakOptions in LineBreaking, LineFill (greedy or balanced), the Hyphen and Ellipsis strings, MaxLines and MaxHeight, a Strut, TrimEdges, TabSize or TabStops with their TabAlignment, the WritingMode and TextOrientation, and the font Fallback. Paragraph.Create prepares the text once: it resolves the styles, finds the bidi levels and break opportunities, splits the text into runs where the bidi level, script, font or a shaping field changes, and shapes each run. Paint fields never split a run, so a color change inside a ligature keeps the ligature. A paragraph is immutable and safe to share between threads. Laying out lines Paragraph.Layout lays a paragraph out at a width and returns a TextLayout: its Width and Height, the LongestLine, and its Lines. Each TextLine has its text range (Start, Length), its line box (Top, Ascent, Descent, Baseline), its content's Left and Width (trailing spaces hang outside it), whether it ends at a HardBreak, and its LayoutRuns in visual order. A run is glyphs (Glyphs, a GlyphRun already at its layout position), a placeholder's box, a tab or a break, by its LayoutRunKind, with its BidiLevel and StyleIndex. ParagraphStyle style = new() { DefaultStyle = new TextStyle { FontFamilies = [family], Size = 16 } }; Paragraph paragraph = Paragraph.Create("A paragraph is shaped once and laid out at any width.", style); // Each width gives an immutable layout: lines of glyph runs, positioned from the box's top-left corner. TextLayout narrow = paragraph.Layout(120); TextLayout wide = paragraph.Layout(400); foreach (TextLine line in narrow.Lines) { string text = paragraph.Text[line.Start..line.End]; // the line's text, its trailing space included float baseline = line.Baseline; // y of the baseline foreach (LayoutRun run in line.Runs) { GlyphRun? glyphs = run.Glyphs; // glyphs at their layout positions } } // No wrapping: the box is as wide as the longest line. TextLayout unbounded = paragraph.Layout(float.PositiveInfinity); Lines fill greedily, as browsers do: each takes the text up to the last break opportunity that fits. A taken soft hyphen shows the Hyphen string, counted in the line's width. A piece too wide for any line overflows, or with OverflowWrap breaks between grapheme clusters. Where a line breaks inside a shaped run at a point the shaper marks unsafe (an Arabic join, a contextual substitution), the pieces on each side are shaped again, so a line has the glyphs it would have on its own. Each line reorders its own bidi runs (UAX #9 rules L1 and L2): trailing spaces take the paragraph's direction. LineFill.Balanced evens the lines of a short paragraph (up to 6 lines): of the breaks that fit, the ones that leave the least squared space on every line, the last included, as Chromium's text-wrap: balance does. float.PositiveInfinity lays the paragraph out without wrapping; the box is then as wide as the longest line. Line boxes and spacing Line boxes follow CSS Inline Layout 3, with the numbers browsers use: Each run's inline box is its font's ascent and descent, rounded to whole units as browsers round them, plus the leading its LineHeight adds: Normal adds the font's line gap, Multiple and Absolute set the height (a computed height is floored to 1/64 unit, browsers' layout unit, so stacked lines do not drift). The leading is split half above and half below, the top half rounded down. A BaselineShift moves the box down (or up, when negative). Every line also holds the root inline box, from the paragraph's DefaultStyle, as CSS's strut does; a Strut adds a minimum box of its own, and with Force it alone sets every line box, for line grids. Placeholders sit by their alignment: on the baseline at an offset, above or below it, or at the middle (half the default font's x-height above the baseline, as CSS's middle); boxes aligned to the line's top or bottom stretch it last. TrimEdges drops the space above the first line's text and below the last one's (CSS text-box-trim). Letter spacing follows each grapheme cluster and word spacing each word separator; tabs advance to the next of the TabStops, which align the text after them at their start, end, centre or first decimal separator, or else to the next multiple of TabSize spaces, at least half a space on. Characters take the first family that has them, as CSS matches fonts, so spaces and punctuation between words of another script stay in the first family. Line boxes equal Chromium's within 0.01 unit on every line-height, strut, spacing, tab, placeholder and mixed-font case, and glyph positions equal its within 0.01 once its 1/64 layout unit is allowed for. Alignment and justification TextAlign places each line: Start and End follow the paragraph's direction, Left, Right and Center do not, and Justify stretches lines to the full width. The last line, and lines before a hard break, use TextAlignLast, whose Auto is the start for justified paragraphs. Trailing spaces hang past the line's end and never count for alignment. TextJustify says where justified lines stretch: InterWord at word separators, InterCharacter between any two grapheme clusters except inside cursive scripts such as Arabic, and Auto (the default) at word separators and around Chinese, Japanese and Korean characters, as browsers justify. None leaves justified lines at the start. Arabic is justified at its word spaces; kashida stretching waits for real demand. Line limits and the ellipsis MaxLines and MaxHeight stop the lines: at the limit, or before the line whose bottom would pass the height. When text is cut, TextLayout.DidExceed is true and HiddenRange says what was hidden; the last kept line drops whole grapheme clusters from its end until its text and the Ellipsis (U+2026 by default, shaped in the style of the last kept character) fit, and the ellipsis ends the line in the paragraph's direction, flagged Ellipsized; a line with room keeps its trailing space before it, as Chromium's line clamp does. A null Ellipsis cuts at the line's end. Ellipses sit where Chromium's -webkit-line-clamp puts them in Latin, Arabic and Chinese. Metrics A TextLayout also answers how big its text is: MinIntrinsicWidth (CSS min-content, the widest piece that cannot break; OverflowWrap.Anywhere lowers it to the widest grapheme cluster) and MaxIntrinsicWidth (max-content, the widest line without wrapping), equal to Chromium's; FirstBaseline and LastBaseline for aligning boxes on text; InkBounds, the union of the glyphs' ink and placeholder boxes, which can reach past the layout box; PlaceholderRects, one TextBounds per placeholder in order, where the caller draws them; and GetLineAt and GetLineAtY to find the line holding a character or a height. Hit testing, carets and selection Editors and selectable text build on four queries, all read-only and safe from any thread: HitTest turns a point into the nearest TextPosition: a UTF-16 index at a grapheme cluster boundary and a TextAffinity that says which side it belongs to where an index has two places (the end of one line and the start of the next, or a direction change). Points outside the lines go to the nearest one; at a direction change, the position is the one the surrounding text gives the edge, as browsers resolve it. GetCaret says where to draw a Caret: its primary CaretLine, and at a bidi boundary a secondary one at the other direction's edge. Inside a ligature, carets use the font's GDEF caret values, or split the ligature evenly by grapheme. MoveCaret steps by CaretMove: grapheme, word, line start and end, paragraph start and end, and line up and down keeping a preferred x across short lines. GetSelectionRects covers a range with rectangles, one per visually contiguous piece on each line, as tall as the line box or, with SelectionHeight.Tight, the fonts' ascent and descent. GetWordBoundary and GetLineBoundary give the word and line around an index. // A click: the nearest caret position, then where to draw the caret. TextPosition position = layout.HitTest(new System.Numerics.Vector2(40, 30)); Caret caret = layout.GetCaret(position); CaretLine bar = caret.Primary; // x, top and bottom; Secondary at a bidi boundary // Arrow keys: logical moves, and line moves that keep the column. TextPosition right = layout.MoveCaret(position, CaretMove.NextGrapheme); TextPosition down = layout.MoveCaret(position, CaretMove.LineDown, preferredX: bar.X); // A selection: rectangles to fill, one per visually contiguous piece on each line. IReadOnlyList<TextBounds> highlight = layout.GetSelectionRects(position.Index, down.Index); Egami.Fonts.Unicode.TextSegment word = layout.GetWordBoundary(position.Index); // double-click Hit tests, carets and selection rectangles equal Chromium's (caretPositionFromPoint, collapsed ranges and Range.getClientRects) on Latin with ligatures, mixed bidi, Arabic, a right-to-left paragraph, emoji, hard breaks and a clamped paragraph. Decorations A TextDecoration on a TextStyle draws underlines, overlines and line-throughs, solid, double, dotted, dashed or wavy. TextLayout.Decorations gives each as a DecorationShape per decorated stretch of a line: one position and thickness for the stretch, and its Segments (each a DecorationSegment from left to right), with gaps cut where glyph ink crosses an underline or overline (SkipInk.Auto, the default; Chinese, Japanese and Korean glyphs never cut). AddTo writes a shape's outline, and TextLayout.ToPath writes the whole layout, glyphs then decorations, to any IGlyphOutlineSink. TextStyle underlined = new() { FontFamilies = [family], Decoration = new TextDecoration { Lines = TextDecorationLines.Underline, Style = TextDecorationStyle.Wavy }, }; TextLayout layout = Paragraph.Create("Typography, quickly", new ParagraphStyle { DefaultStyle = underlined }).Layout(400); foreach (DecorationShape line in layout.Decorations) { // Top and Thickness place the line; Segments skip the descenders of y, p, g and q. System.Console.WriteLine($"{line.Line} at {line.Top}: {line.Segments.Count} pieces"); } // Or everything as outlines, to fill with any path renderer. PathRecorder path = new(); layout.ToPath(path); Positions follow Chromium's text-decoration rules rather than the font's underline values: the thickness is a tenth of the font size, floored to whole pixels; the underline sits half a thickness below the baseline (or UnderlineOffset below it); the overline on the ascent; the line-through a third of the ascent up. Thicknesses, positions and skip-ink gaps equal Chromium's ink within half a pixel on sans and serif text. Vertical layouts have no decorations yet. Drawing paragraphs Canvas.DrawTextLayout (Egami.Drawing) draws a layout with its top-left corner at a point, line by line in CSS's order: text shadows, run backgrounds, underlines and overlines, glyphs and placeholders, then line-throughs. A run's paint is its style's Paint (an Egami.Drawing Paint) or Color; shadows blur with a standard deviation of half their blur radius, as CSS. Lines outside the clip or the optional visible rectangle are skipped, and a PlaceholderPainter draws each placeholder in its box. Canvas.DrawText into a RectF lays out and draws in one call, placing the lines by VerticalAlign, and TextLayout.ToPath(origin) gives glyphs and decorations as one Path. On a PDF canvas the glyph runs keep their text, and an ellipsis or a soft hyphen's hyphen is marked content whose ActualText is the text it stands for. ParagraphStyle style = new() { DefaultStyle = new TextStyle { FontFamilies = [family], Size = 18, Color = new Rgba8(30, 30, 60, 255), Shadows = [new TextShadow(new System.Numerics.Vector2(1, 1), 2, new Rgba8(0, 0, 0, 80))], }, Align = TextAlign.Justify, }; // One call: wrap into a box, centred across the lines. TextLayout boxed = canvas.DrawText("Paragraphs wrap, justify and drop shadows.", new RectF(10, 10, 300, 80), style, VerticalAlign.Center); // Or lay out once and draw where needed, skipping lines outside the visible part. TextLayout layout = Paragraph.Create("Laid out once, drawn many times.", style).Layout(300); canvas.DrawTextLayout(layout, new System.Numerics.Vector2(10, 110), visibleRect: new RectF(0, 0, 320, 200)); // Inline placeholders (an icon, a badge) are drawn by a painter called with each one's box. canvas.DrawTextLayout(layout, new System.Numerics.Vector2(10, 130), placeholderPainter: (c, index, box) => c.FillRoundRect(new RoundRect(box, 3), new Rgba8(200, 60, 40, 255))); // The same text as one path: glyphs and decorations. Egami.Drawing.Path outline = layout.ToPath(new System.Numerics.Vector2(10, 150)); Vertical lines WritingMode.VerticalRl stacks top-to-bottom lines from right to left, as Chinese and Japanese books, and VerticalLr from left to right. TextOrientation.Mixed (the default) stands each character as UAX #50's Vertical_Orientation says: Chinese, Japanese and Korean upright, shaped top to bottom with the font's vertical metrics and alternates, and Latin turned a quarter clockwise on the central baseline; Upright stands everything upright and Sideways turns whole lines. The width given to Layout is the lines' length; the layout's Height is that length and its Width the columns added up. Along a line, positions are y (a line's Left and Width, a run's X, a caret's X), across the lines x (a line's Top, Baseline and Bottom); glyph runs and rectangles stay in x and y. Line breaks, line boxes, positions, hit tests, carets and selections equal Chromium's writing-mode output on Japanese, Chinese and mixed Latin. LineFlow lays a paragraph out one line at a time, each at its own width, to flow text across columns and pages or around images: Paragraph.CreateFlow, then NextLine until it returns null. Each line's top is 0; place it where it goes, and Rewind to a line's start to take back a line that does not fit. // One line at a time, each at its own width: two columns of four lines, the second wrapping around an image. LineFlow flow = paragraph.CreateFlow(); List<TextLine> first = [], second = []; while (first.Count < 4 && flow.NextLine(150) is TextLine line) { first.Add(line); } while (flow.NextLine(second.Count < 2 ? 90 : 150) is TextLine line) { second.Add(line); // narrower beside the image } Line breaks equal headless Chromium's on a corpus of eleven scripts at five widths each, and on the feature cases; the few differences are Chromium's own (its older quotation mark rule, no break at U+2028, no break after a slash in URLs, letter spacing in Arabic).

articles/guides/pixel-types.html.title: Pixel types | Egami
articles/guides/pixel-types.html.summary: Pixel types A raster stores one pixel type, chosen when you load or create it. Pick the type your data is in, or the one you will work in: loading straight into it converts row by row while decoding, with no full-size copy in between. // Load straight into the type you will work in: the decoder converts row by row, with no full-size copy in between. using Raster<Rgb16> deep = Raster.Load<Rgb16>("duck.png"); // 16 bits a channel, no alpha using Raster<Alpha8> mask = Raster.Load<Alpha8>("duck.png"); // only the alpha channel using Raster<RgbaF16> half = Raster.Load<RgbaF16>("duck.png"); // half floats, room for HDR values // Or convert a raster you have; conversions between integer types are exact wherever the target can hold the value. using Raster<Bgr565> display = deep.As<Bgr565>(); The types Type Bytes Holds Typical use Rgba8, Bgra8 4 8-bit color, straight alpha The default working type; Windows and GPU buffers Argb8, Abgr8 4 8-bit color, alpha first Java and other alpha-first buffers Rgb8, Bgr8 3 8-bit color Photos without alpha Gray8, GrayAlpha8 1, 2 8-bit gray Grayscale images Alpha8 1 Alpha only Masks, glyph coverage Rgba16, Rgb16 8, 6 16-bit color, with or without alpha 16-bit PNG, PPM and TIFF Gray16, GrayAlpha16 2, 4 16-bit gray 16-bit gray PNG and PAM RgbaF32, RgbF32, GrayF32 16, 12, 4 32-bit float Precise processing, PFM, depth and height maps RgbaF16 8 16-bit half float HDR, GPU textures Bgr565, Bgra4444, Rgb10A2 2, 2, 4 Packed color Embedded displays, legacy textures, 10-bit displays Cmyk8, Cmyk16 4, 8 Ink amounts CMYK JPEG, TIFF and PSD PremulRgba8, PremulBgra8, PremulRgbaF32 4, 4, 16 Color premultiplied by alpha Compositing, Windows and GPU surfaces Packed types are named after their channels from the lowest bit up, as DXGI and Vulkan name formats, so a Direct3D or Vulkan texture wraps without a swizzle: Bgr565 has blue in bits 0 to 4 and red in 11 to 15, the same memory as Skia's and Android's RGB 565. Conversions Every type converts to every other with raster.As<TPixel>() or, for a span, PixelConvert.Convert. Conversions between integer types are exact wherever the target can hold the value: 8 to 16 bits multiplies by 257, packed levels round to the nearest value both ways, and 16 to 8 bits rounds to nearest, so every value of a narrower type survives a round trip through a wider one. Half floats round as (Half)f does. Values are sRGB-encoded with straight alpha. Gray types take the Rec. 709 luma in linear light; Alpha8 reads as black with its alpha, and converting a color to it keeps only alpha. Half and float types keep values outside 0..1 through conversions, geometry and saving to PFM; filters and color adjustments work in 0..1 and clip, as they do for RgbaF32. // Half and float types keep values above 1 through conversions and geometry; filters and color adjustments clip to 0..1. using Raster<RgbaF16> light = Raster.Create<RgbaF16>(64, 64, RgbaF16.FromScaled(new Vector4(4f, 2f, 0.5f, 1f))); light.Apply(ops => ops.FlipHorizontal().Pad(80, 80, Rgba8.Black)); // PFM keeps floats as they are: save as RGB floats, in linear light by convention. light.Save("light.pfm"); using Raster<RgbF32> back = Raster.Load<RgbF32>("light.pfm"); Console.WriteLine($"Red is still {back.Row(40)[40].R} after the round trip"); CMYK Cmyk8 and Cmyk16 hold ink amounts, 0 meaning no ink. Until Egami applies ICC profiles, they convert to and from RGB with the plain formula, red = (1 − C)(1 − K) — what the JPEG reader has always used — so print-accurate color needs the file's profile. // A CMYK JPEG loads as RGB by the plain formula, as before; ask for Cmyk8 to get the file's ink amounts instead. using Raster<Cmyk8> inks = Raster.Load<Cmyk8>("duck-cmyk.jpg"); Cmyk8 corner = inks.Row(0)[0]; Console.WriteLine($"Cyan {corner.C}, magenta {corner.M}, yellow {corner.Y}, black {corner.K} (0 = no ink)"); // Resizing filters the four inks, so black stays in the black channel; color adjustments go through RGB instead. inks.Apply(ops => ops.Fit(160, 160)); Moving pixels (crop, pad, flip, turning by 90°) copies inks. Resize, blur, sharpen, convolution and free rotation filter the four inks as numbers, so black stays in the black channel. Color adjustments are defined on RGB, so they convert to RGB and back and rebuild black from the formula. DrawImage onto a CMYK raster turns the source's color into inks and blends inks. Premultiplied alpha The Premul types store each color channel multiplied by alpha, as Skia and GPU surfaces do. Their conversions still take and return straight colors, so loading, saving and converting work as for any type. Resize, blur, convolution, rotation and DrawImage run on the stored values directly, without multiplying and dividing per pixel: on translucent images resize is about 30% and DrawImage about 35% faster than on Rgba8. // A Windows or GPU surface is premultiplied BGRA: wrap its memory as PremulBgra8 and draw into it directly. Drawing and // resizing run on the stored values, with no multiply and divide per pixel; conversions still take straight colors. using Raster<PremulBgra8> surface = Raster.Wrap<PremulBgra8>(surfaceMemory, 320, 240, byteStride: 320 * 4); using Raster<Rgba8> logo = Raster.Load<Rgba8>("duck.png"); logo.Apply(ops => ops.Fit(120, 120)); surface.Apply(ops => ops.FillColor(new Rgba8(30, 60, 90, 255)).DrawImage(logo, new Point(20, 20), opacity: 0.8f)); Unpremultiplying loses precision where alpha is low (a color at alpha 10 has 11 levels), so keep straight types for images you will edit color by color. Packed types // A 16-bit display framebuffer: wrap it as Bgr565 and draw a photo into it; each level rounds to the nearest of 32 or 64. using Raster<Bgr565> screen = Raster.Wrap<Bgr565>(MemoryMarshal.Cast<ushort, Bgr565>(framebuffer.AsSpan()).ToArray(), 240, 135); using Raster<Rgba8> photo = Raster.Load<Rgba8>("egret.png"); photo.Apply(ops => ops.Cover(240, 135)); screen.Apply(ops => ops.DrawImage(photo, new Point(0, 0))); Bgr565 pixel = screen.Row(60)[120]; Console.WriteLine($"Levels: red {pixel.R} of 31, green {pixel.G} of 63, blue {pixel.B} of 31"); Bgr565, Bgra4444 and Rgb10A2 keep their bits in Value, with level constructors and properties for each channel. BMP files with 5-6-5 or 4-4-4-4 bit fields read straight into them. Your own pixel type Implement IPixelType<TSelf> on an unmanaged struct. Layout says how it is stored: a packed layout gives its pixel size and channel widths with new PixelLayoutInfo(order, PixelChannelType.Packed, alpha, bitsPerPixel, widths...), and a layout Egami has no name for uses PixelChannelOrder.Other. The 16-bit members ToRgba16 and FromRgba16 have default bodies; override them with exact integer code if your type is wider than 8 bits. See custom operations and formats. Run it samples/PixelTypes is a console app that does what this guide shows on the bundled images: dotnet run --project samples/PixelTypes writes its results to ./output.

articles/guides/planar-yuv.html.title: Planar YUV | Egami
articles/guides/planar-yuv.html.summary: Planar YUV A YuvRaster holds a picture as separate luma (Y) and chroma (U, V) planes, plus an optional alpha plane: the way video codecs, AVIF, lossy WebP and JPEG store it. Use it to take frames from a decoder or a camera, to scale video before converting it, and to read and write JPEG without the RGB step. Everything else is done on a Raster after conversion. Creating and wrapping // A 1080p frame as video stores it: full-size luma, chroma at half width and height, BT.709 at limited range. using YuvRaster<byte> frame = YuvRaster.Create(1920, 1080, ChromaFormat.Yuv420, YuvColor.Bt709Limited); // 10-bit HDR planes hold samples 0 to 1023 in ushorts; an alpha plane is optional. using YuvRaster<ushort> hdr = YuvRaster.Create(3840, 2160, ChromaFormat.Yuv420, 10, YuvColor.Bt2020Limited, alpha: true); Console.WriteLine($"Chroma planes are {frame.U!.Width}×{frame.U.Height}"); Each plane is a YuvPlane<TSample>. YuvRaster<byte> holds 8-bit samples; YuvRaster<ushort> holds 10-, 12- or 16-bit samples, stored low-bit aligned (a 10-bit sample is 0 to 1023), as libvpx, dav1d and libavif hand them out. Chroma planes are half the luma width (4:2:0 and 4:2:2) and half the height (4:2:0), rounded up; 4:0:0 has no chroma at all. The planes come from the context's memory source in one block, so pooling, SafetyLimits and the usage counters cover them. using YuvRaster<byte> yuv = YuvRaster.Create(640, 480, ChromaFormat.Yuv420, YuvColor.Jpeg); // Planes are read and written by row, like a raster's pixels. for (int y = 0; y < yuv.Y.Height; y++) { yuv.Y.Row(y).Fill((byte)(y / 2)); } yuv.U!.Row(0)[0] = 128; // An 8-bit plane can be viewed as Gray8 pixels, without copying. PixelPlane<Gray8> luma = yuv.Y.AsGray8(); Frames a decoder or the operating system already holds are wrapped without a copy: // A decoder's 10-bit frame, rows padded to 64 samples: wrapped without a copy. Disposing the raster disposes the owner. int width = 50, height = 30, stride = 64, chromaStride = 32; ushort[] y = new ushort[stride * height], u = new ushort[chromaStride * 15], v = new ushort[chromaStride * 15]; using YuvRaster<ushort> wrapped = YuvRaster.Wrap<ushort>( y, stride, u, chromaStride, v, chromaStride, width, height, ChromaFormat.Yuv420, bitDepth: 10, YuvColor.Bt2020Limited, owner: null); What the samples mean // How samples turn into RGB is always stated: a preset, or the codes a video container carries (ITU-T H.273). YuvColor jpeg = YuvColor.Jpeg; // BT.601, full range, chroma centered YuvColor custom = new(YuvMatrix.Bt709, YuvRange.Full, ChromaSiting.Left); if (YuvColor.TryFromH273(matrixCoefficients: 9, fullRange: false, ChromaSiting.TopLeft, out YuvColor fromStream)) { Console.WriteLine($"{fromStream.Matrix}, {fromStream.Range}; back to code {fromStream.ToH273()}"); } // Or straight from the code points an AVIF or PNG cICP box carries. Egami.Colors.ColorCodePoints hdr10 = new(Primaries: 9, TransferCharacteristics: 16, MatrixCoefficients: 9, FullRange: false); hdr10.TryGetYuvColor(ChromaSiting.TopLeft, out YuvColor fromBox); Part Values Notes YuvMatrix Bt601, Bt709, Bt2020Ncl, Identity Kr and Kb from ITU-T H.273. Identity stores G, B, R as Y, U, V (AV1 lossless) YuvRange Full, Limited Limited is luma 16 to 235 and chroma 16 to 240 at 8 bits, scaled for more ChromaSiting Center, Left, TopLeft JPEG and WebP center chroma; BT.601 and BT.709 video put it on the left column; BT.2020 on the top-left sample There is no default guess: every load, wrap and conversion states a YuvColor. YuvColor.TryFromH273 reads the matrix_coefficients code and full-range flag that AV1, VP9, HEVC and CICP boxes carry, and refuses codes Egami does not know; ColorCodePoints.TryGetYuvColor does the same from code points already read. Converting using Raster photo = Raster.Load("duck.png"); // RGB to planes and back. RGB comes out in the picture's own transfer (BT.709 video gives BT.709-encoded RGB). using YuvRaster<byte> yuv = YuvRaster.FromRaster(photo, ChromaFormat.Yuv420, YuvColor.Bt709Limited); using Raster rgba = yuv.ToRaster(); // Rgba8 for 8-bit planes, Rgba16 for more using Raster<Rgb8> rgb = yuv.ToRaster<Rgb8>(); // or any pixel type FromRaster drops alpha unless asked: pass alpha: true for an alpha plane, opaque when the source has none. Conversion is within one level of an exact double-precision implementation of H.273, at every depth, and identical for at least 99% of samples. RGB comes out in the picture's own transfer function: BT.709 video gives BT.709-encoded RGB, PQ gives PQ-encoded RGB. Linearizing or tone mapping is a separate step (see color management). Chroma is filtered by its siting both ways: bilinear upsampling (the 3:1 triangle filter for centered chroma, the average between co-sited samples otherwise), and averaging that matches the siting on the way back. The fast options repeat or pick samples instead: using Raster photo = Raster.Load("duck.png"); // The defaults filter chroma by its siting both ways; Nearest and Fast trade edge quality for speed. YuvConvertOptions fast = new() { Upsampling = ChromaUpsampling.Nearest, Downsampling = ChromaDownsampling.Fast }; using YuvRaster<byte> yuv = YuvRaster.FromRaster(photo, ChromaFormat.Yuv420, YuvColor.Bt601Limited, options: fast); using Raster<Rgba8> back = yuv.ToRaster<Rgba8>(fast); A player converts every frame into the same raster; after the first frame nothing is allocated: // A player converts every frame into the same raster: after the first frame, nothing is allocated. using YuvRaster<byte> frame = YuvRaster.Create(1280, 720, ChromaFormat.Yuv420, YuvColor.Bt709Limited); using Raster<Bgra8> screen = Raster.Create<Bgra8>(1280, 720); for (int i = 0; i < 3; i++) { // ... the decoder writes frame's planes ... frame.CopyTo(screen); } // And the other way, for an encoder: CopyFrom fills existing planes. frame.CopyFrom(screen); Interleaved layouts Media Foundation, MediaCodec, GPU decoders and webcams hand out NV12, NV21, P010, P016, YUYV or UYVY. One SIMD pass copies them to and from the planes: // An NV12 frame from Media Foundation or MediaCodec: Y rows, then interleaved U, V rows, both at the same stride. int width = 640, height = 360, stride = 704; byte[] nv12 = new byte[stride * height * 3 / 2]; using YuvRaster<byte> frame = YuvRaster.Create(width, height, ChromaFormat.Yuv420, YuvColor.Bt709Limited); frame.CopyFromPacked(YuvPackedFormat.Nv12, nv12, stride); // A webcam's YUYV, 4:2:2 in one plane, the other way. using YuvRaster<byte> webcam = YuvRaster.Create(width, height, ChromaFormat.Yuv422, YuvColor.Bt601Limited); byte[] yuyv = new byte[width * 2 * height]; webcam.CopyToPacked(YuvPackedFormat.Yuyv, yuyv); JPEG without the RGB step // A JPEG's own planes, as decoded: no chroma upsampling and no color conversion. YuvRasterInfo info = YuvRaster.Probe("duck.jpg"); Console.WriteLine($"{info.Info.Width}×{info.Info.Height}, planes: {info.ChromaFormat}"); using YuvRaster planes = YuvRaster.Load("duck.jpg"); // Saving JPEG-colored 8-bit planes skips color conversion and downsampling; other planes are converted first. planes.Save("copy.jpg", new JpegWriterOptions { Quality = 90 }); YuvRaster.Load gives a YCbCr JPEG's planes exactly as libjpeg-turbo's raw output does: 4:2:0, 4:2:2 or 4:4:4 at the file's own sampling (other samplings are replicated to 4:4:4), gray as 4:0:0, also at reduced scale. CMYK, YCCK and RGB JPEGs, and formats without planes, throw NotSupportedException: load those with Raster.Load. Saving 8-bit BT.601 full-range planes as JPEG encodes them straight, with the same bytes as libjpeg-turbo's encoder from planes. Loading planes skips chroma upsampling and color conversion, so it is faster than Raster.Load on one thread. On several threads both are limited by the same Huffman decoding and take about the same time. Converting loaded planes with ToRaster may differ by one level, in a small share of pixels, from Raster.Load, which keeps the JPEG decoder's own libjpeg-turbo color code. Crop and resize using YuvRaster<byte> frame = YuvRaster.Create(1920, 1080, ChromaFormat.Yuv420, YuvColor.Bt709Limited); // Scale the planes before converting, as video does; crops start on a chroma sample (even x and y at 4:2:0). using YuvRaster<byte> small = frame.Resize(1280, 720, ResampleFilter.Bicubic); using YuvRaster<byte> center = small.Crop(new Rect(320, 180, 640, 360)); // A player scales every frame into the same raster. using YuvRaster<byte> screen = YuvRaster.Create(960, 540, ChromaFormat.Yuv420, YuvColor.Bt709Limited); frame.ResizeTo(screen); // Everything else (rotate, color adjustments, drawing) runs on a Raster after conversion. using Raster<Rgba8> rgb = center.ToRaster<Rgba8>(); rgb.Apply(ops => ops.Rotate(90)); Resize runs each plane through the same filters as RasterOps.Resize and clamps to the bit depth; the chroma format, siting and color stay. For now it is somewhat slower than resizing the same picture as Rgba8, whose resize has a faster horizontal pass. ResizeTo does the same into a raster you already have, so a player scales every frame into one raster. Crop must start on a chroma sample, so chroma is copied exactly.

articles/guides/psd.html.title: PSD and PSB | Egami
articles/guides/psd.html.summary: PSD and PSB Egami reads Adobe Photoshop documents (.psd) and large documents (.psb), written from Adobe's Photoshop File Format Specification. PsdFormat.Info is registered in EgamiContext.Default; PSD is never written. Egami reads the flattened image Photoshop stores after the layers, in every color mode and depth, and lists the layers as metadata without their pixels. Reading files // Load gives the flattened image Photoshop stores after the layers, in the type that fits the file: Rgb8 here, Rgba16 for // a 16-bit file with transparency, Cmyk8 for CMYK. Save it as anything. using Raster flat = Raster.Load("layered.psd"); flat.Save("layered.png"); // The ICC profile, resolution, EXIF, XMP and IPTC are in the metadata as for every format. using Raster photo = Raster.Load("photo.psd"); ReadOnlyMemory<byte> icc = photo.Metadata.IccProfile; Resolution? dpi = photo.Metadata.Resolution; Color mode 1-bit 8-bit 16-bit 32-bit Bitmap Gray8, 1 black Grayscale, duotone Gray8, GrayAlpha8 Gray16, GrayAlpha16 GrayF32; RgbaF32 with alpha Indexed Rgb8; Rgba8 with a transparent index RGB Rgb8, Rgba8 Rgb16, Rgba16 RgbF32, RgbaF32 CMYK Cmyk8; Rgba8 with alpha Cmyk16; Rgba16 with alpha Lab Rgb8, Rgba8, converted to sRGB Rgb16, Rgba16 Multichannel Gray8 of the first channel Gray16 CMYK loads as ink amounts, with the file's ICC profile, so ConvertColorTo and ConvertColor turn it into RGB through the profile as for a CMYK JPEG; with transparency it loads as RGBA by the plain formula. Lab is converted to sRGB from D50 by Bradford, as for TIFF's CIELab. 32-bit files are linear light and say so in RasterMetadata.ColorSpace, or carry the file's profile. A duotone file loads as its gray channel, its inks kept in PsdDetails.ColorModeData; a multichannel file has no color model, so its first channel loads as gray with the Psd.ChannelsDropped warning. Transparency is the channel after the color ones when the layer count is negative, as Photoshop marks it; Photoshop stores the flattened image flattened onto white, and the white is divided back out, so colors under partial transparency come out as painted. ImageMagick does the same for RGB files only, and Pillow not at all. Other extra channels (alpha and spot channels) are not loaded; their names are in PsdDetails.ExtraChannels. PsdDetails says what the file is: PSD or PSB (Version), its PsdColorMode, bits a channel, channel count and the PsdCompression of the flattened image. The image resources map to metadata: the ICC profile (1039), resolution (1005), EXIF (1058, whose orientation reaches RasterInfo.Orientation), XMP (1060) and IPTC (1028). Every other resource, the thumbnail (1036) among them, is kept as it was read in PsdDetails.OtherResources. using Raster image = Raster.Load("photo.psd"); var details = (PsdDetails)image.Metadata.FormatDetails!; Console.WriteLine($"{(details.Version == 2 ? "PSB" : "PSD")}, {details.ColorMode} at {details.BitsPerChannel} bits, {details.ChannelCount} channels, {details.Compression}"); if (!details.HasRealComposite) { // Saved without Maximize Compatibility: what loaded is Photoshop's placeholder, and a warning says so. Console.WriteLine("Save the file again with Maximize Compatibility on."); } foreach (PsdResource resource in details.OtherResources) { Console.WriteLine($"Resource {resource.Id}, {resource.Data.Length} bytes"); } No real composite A file saved without Photoshop's Maximize Compatibility holds no real flattened image, only a placeholder. Egami loads it with the Psd.NoComposite warning and PsdDetails.HasRealComposite false; it does not composite the layers itself, which would need Photoshop's blend modes, adjustment layers, effects and text. ImageMagick flattens the layers instead. Layers PsdDetails.Layers lists the layer records bottom to top as the file does: name (the Unicode name when there is one), bounds, opacity (0 to 1, as DrawImage takes it), blend mode (Photoshop's key and Egami's BlendMode where there is one), visibility, clipping, and whether the record is a layer or one end of a group, with its nesting level. Their pixels are not loaded; LoadAll returns the flattened image only. // Layer records come as metadata, bottom to top as the file lists them; their pixels are not loaded. using Raster image = Raster.Load("layered.psd"); foreach (PsdLayer layer in ((PsdDetails)image.Metadata.FormatDetails!).Layers) { if (layer.Kind == PsdLayerKind.GroupEnd) { continue; } string kind = layer.Kind == PsdLayerKind.Layer ? "layer" : "group"; Console.WriteLine($"{new string(' ', 2 * layer.Level)}{layer.Name} ({kind}, {layer.BlendModeKey}, opacity {layer.Opacity:P0}{(layer.IsVisible ? "" : ", hidden")})"); } Streaming and speed Rows come from the channel planes as they are asked for: raw rows at computed offsets and PackBits rows through their byte counts, read where they lie on a seekable stream, so Region reads only the rows it needs and the layer data is skipped without being read. A stream that cannot seek is read to its end first, and Deflate data is inflated whole. On 12-megapixel files Egami decodes three to ten times faster than ImageMagick (Magick.NET). Damaged and hostile data The header's size is checked against SafetyLimits before anything else; PSB's sides of up to 300,000 pixels stay behind the default limits unless the caller raises them. Every section length is checked against the data that remains, the layer section is skipped by its length, the image resources and layer records count against MaxMetadataBytes, and the PackBits row table is bounded by the header before it is read. Damaged layer records or resources are warnings (Psd.LayersDamaged, Psd.ResourcesDamaged), since the flattened image does not depend on them. Image data that ends early loads with the missing pixels 0 and the Psd.DataTruncated warning, and throws CorruptDataException in strict mode. The reader is fuzzed with AFL++ through whole files and through the image data alone.

articles/guides/regions-and-masks.html.title: Regions, masks and channels | Egami
articles/guides/regions-and-masks.html.summary: Regions, masks and channels Any chain that keeps the image's size can run on part of the image: inside a rectangle with Within(Rect, …), or through a gray mask with Within(Mask, …). The inner chain is the same lambda Apply and Derive take. A rectangle // Blur a face: only pixels inside the rectangle change, and the blur reads the real pixels around it, so there is no seam. photo.Apply(ops => ops .Within(new Rect(200, 120, 160, 120), o => o.Blur(6)) .Within(new Rect(0, 0, photo.Width, 60), o => o.Brightness(0.8f).Saturation(0.5f)), Ct); // a darker band on top Only pixels inside the rectangle change. It is clipped to the image; one that misses it changes nothing. Filters read the real pixels around the rectangle, so a blurred rectangle has no seam: inside, it equals the whole-image blur. Positions inside the scope (DrawImage, FillColor) are the image's coordinates, as outside it. Flips and a 180° turn mirror the rectangle itself. A step that changes the size (resize, crop, pad, a 90° or free turn, AutoOrient) or the color encoding (ConvertColor, ToneMap) throws ArgumentException when the chain is recorded, naming the step, before any pixel changes. Custom operations work inside a scope without changes: they run on a copy of the area and see it as their whole image. A mask // Edit only the sky: a gray mask, white where the edit applies fully, black where it does not, soft in between. photo.Apply(ops => ops .Within(new Mask(sky), o => o.Saturation(1.3f).Contrast(1.1f)) // Or take coverage from a logo's alpha, placed on the photo, and invert the area under it. .Within(new Mask(logo, new Point(20, 20), MaskChannel.Alpha), o => o.Invert()), Ct); A Mask reads coverage from any raster: a one-channel raster's value (gray, or Alpha8's alpha) by default, otherwise its alpha, otherwise its luminance; MaskChannel picks a channel explicitly. Offset places it, Inverted flips it, and outside the raster coverage is 0 (full when inverted). The result is mixed with the original by coverage on premultiplied pixels: 0 keeps the original exactly, full keeps the result exactly, and a transparent result leaves no color fringe. Only the box around the mask's non-zero coverage is touched, found once when the chain is planned. Coverage is 8-bit for 8-bit images and float for 16-bit and float ones, so a 16-bit mask keeps its gradient on a 16-bit photo. Masking an image with itself reads the mask from a copy. A soft edge is the mask's own business: blur the mask raster first for a feathered selection. Channels ExtractChannel pulls one channel (ColorChannel: red, green, blue, alpha or luminance) out as a gray raster, Gray8 from 8-bit images, Gray16 from 16-bit ones and GrayF32 from float ones; CombineChannels builds an image from three or four gray rasters. Both equal ImageMagick's -separate and -combine at 8 and 16 bits. // Pull channels out as gray rasters (Gray8 from 8-bit images), edit one, and build the image again. using Raster red = photo.ExtractChannel(ColorChannel.Red); using Raster green = photo.ExtractChannel(ColorChannel.Green); using Raster blue = photo.ExtractChannel(ColorChannel.Blue); blue.Apply(ops => ops.Blur(2), Ct); using Raster<Rgba8> rebuilt = Raster.CombineChannels<Rgba8>(red, green, blue); ShuffleChannels rearranges channels in place, each output channel taking an input channel or a constant (ChannelSource). It is a color matrix, so it fuses with Brightness, Contrast and the other color steps. // Swap red and blue: one color matrix, fused with the other color steps into one pass. photo.Apply(ops => ops .ShuffleChannels(ChannelSource.Blue, ChannelSource.Green, ChannelSource.Red, ChannelSource.Alpha) .Brightness(1.05f), Ct); OnChannels is a scope like Within: the chain runs, and its result is kept only in the chosen channels (ColorChannels). Color steps alone become one matrix with the other channels left alone, so they cost nothing extra. // Soften only the alpha; invert only the red. photo.Apply(ops => ops .OnChannels(ColorChannels.Alpha, o => o.Blur(2)) .OnChannels(ColorChannels.Red, o => o.Invert()), Ct); Alpha AlphaToGray shows alpha as gray (ImageMagick's -alpha extract), LuminanceToAlpha turns brightness into alpha (-alpha copy), CopyAlpha takes alpha from a mask, and Flatten composites onto a background color and makes the image opaque (-alpha remove). The JPEG writer's Background option flattens with the same arithmetic. using Raster alpha = photo.Derive(ops => ops.AlphaToGray(), Ct); // see the transparency as gray using Raster cutout = photo.Derive(ops => ops.CopyAlpha(new Mask(matte)), Ct); // a gray image becomes the alpha using Raster onWhite = cutout.Derive(ops => ops.Flatten(Rgba8.White), Ct); // composite onto white, opaque using Raster luma = photo.Derive(ops => ops.LuminanceToAlpha(), Ct); // brightness becomes alpha Nesting Scopes nest: a rectangle inside a rectangle is their intersection, a mask inside a mask multiplies the coverage, and rectangles and masks combine in either order. Cost A rectangle costs nothing beyond the work inside it; a filter reads only the band of rows and columns around the area its kernel reaches.
