articles/guides/unicode-text.html.summary: Unicode text and shaping Egami.Fonts carries its own Unicode 17.0 data and the Unicode algorithms text shaping builds on: character properties, the bidirectional algorithm and text boundaries, in the Egami.Fonts.Unicode namespace. On top of them, Egami.Fonts.Shaping shapes text with a font's OpenType tables, as HarfBuzz does, with HarfBuzz's script shapers (Arabic, Syriac, N'Ko and Mongolian joining, Hebrew, the nine Indic scripts, Khmer, Myanmar, Thai, Lao, Hangul, and the Universal Shaping Engine for Tibetan, Sinhala, Javanese and the other complex scripts), itemization, font fallback and drawing on the canvas. The tables are generated from the Unicode Character Database by tools/make-unicode-tables.py and never come from the .NET runtime, so the same text gives the same answer on every runtime and machine. UnicodeData.UnicodeVersion says which version they follow. Character properties UnicodeData answers per code point: the general category (as the runtime's UnicodeCategory), the Script and its script extensions, the BidiClass, the mirroring character and BidiPairedBracketType, the JoiningType and JoiningGroup of Arabic and Syriac letters, the canonical combining class, the VerticalOrientation, the EastAsianWidth, the LineBreakClass (UAX #14), the emoji properties and whether a character is default ignorable. // Egami's own Unicode 17.0 tables: the same answer on every runtime and machine. Script script = UnicodeData.GetScript('\u0915'); // Devanagari ReadOnlySpan<FontTag> tags = script.OpenTypeTags; // dev2, then deva BidiClass bidi = UnicodeData.GetBidiClass('\u0627'); // ArabicLetter JoiningType joining = UnicodeData.GetJoiningType('\u0628'); // DualJoining JoiningGroup group = UnicodeData.GetJoiningGroup('\u0628'); // Beh VerticalOrientation upright = UnicodeData.GetVerticalOrientation('\u6F22'); // Upright EastAsianWidth width = UnicodeData.GetEastAsianWidth('\u6F22'); // Wide bool emoji = UnicodeData.IsEmojiPresentation(0x1F600); // true UnicodeData.TryGetBidiMirroringGlyph('(', out int mirror); // ')' BidiPairedBracketType bracket = UnicodeData.GetBidiPairedBracketType('['); // Open A Script has its ISO 15924 Code, its Unicode Name and the OpenType tags fonts use for it, newest first (dev2 then deva). Common, Inherited and Unknown are the shared scripts, and fonts know them as DFLT. Every lookup is a few array reads and allocates nothing. Code points run from 0 to 0x10FFFF; lone surrogates are code points too. Bidirectional text Bidi.Resolve runs the Unicode Bidirectional Algorithm (UAX #9) in full: embeddings, overrides and isolates up to depth 125, paired brackets and the weak and neutral rules. It returns a BidiResult with a level per UTF-16 unit and the BidiRuns of equal level; Reorder gives one line's runs from left to right. TextDirection.Auto, the default, takes each paragraph's direction from its first strong character; LeftToRight and RightToLeft force it. // A Hebrew word inside English text: three runs, the middle one drawn right to left. string text = "abc \u05D0\u05D1\u05D2 def"; using BidiResult result = Bidi.Resolve(text, TextDirection.Auto); int paragraph = result.ParagraphLevel; // 0: the first strong character is Latin foreach (BidiRun run in result.Reorder(0, result.Length)) { Console.WriteLine($"{run.Start}+{run.Length} {(run.IsRightToLeft ? "right to left" : "left to right")}"); } Each paragraph separator ends a paragraph, and each paragraph is resolved on its own. Levels lays each paragraph out as one line. When text is wrapped, call Reorder per line: trailing spaces then take the paragraph's level, as rule L1 asks. The result rents its arrays; dispose it when done. Unicode's BidiTest.txt and BidiCharacterTest.txt pass in full. Graphemes and words TextSegmenter.Graphemes walks extended grapheme clusters (UAX #29): what a reader sees as one character, such as a letter with its accents, a Hangul syllable, a Devanagari conjunct or an emoji sequence. TextSegmenter.Words walks the segments between word boundaries with Unicode's default rules. Both return a TextSegment per segment through a GraphemeEnumerator or WordEnumerator that allocates nothing; IsGraphemeBoundary checks one index. // A family emoji is one grapheme cluster of eight UTF-16 units; "can't" is one word. string text = "\uD83D\uDC68\u200D\uD83D\uDC69\u200D\uD83D\uDC67 can't stop"; var graphemes = new List<TextSegment>(); foreach (TextSegment grapheme in TextSegmenter.Graphemes(text)) { graphemes.Add(grapheme); } var words = new List<string>(); foreach (TextSegment word in TextSegmenter.Words(text)) { words.Add(text.Substring(word.Start, word.Length)); } bool inside = TextSegmenter.IsGraphemeBoundary(text, 2); // false: inside the family Words use no dictionary, so Thai, Lao, Khmer and CJK text without spaces is not split into words. Line breaking (UAX #14) arrives with paragraph layout in 2.8.2. Unicode's GraphemeBreakTest.txt and WordBreakTest.txt pass in full. Shaping a run TextShaper.ShapeRun shapes one run of text in one font, as HarfBuzz's hb_shape: the font's GSUB substitutions (ligatures, contextual and alternate forms) and GPOS positioning (kerning, marks, cursive attachment) with the default features, normalization against the font's character map, and the fallbacks HarfBuzz uses for fonts that lack them. RunProperties gives the script (taken from the text when null), a BCP 47 language (none by default: the font's default forms, never the machine's culture), the direction, feature settings and the ClusterLevel. The result lands in a reusable GlyphBuffer: glyph ids, the UTF-16 index each glyph's cluster starts at, GlyphFlags and a GlyphPosition per glyph, in visual order and in the font's units. // One run, one font, as HarfBuzz's hb_shape: ligatures, kerning and marks from the font's GSUB and GPOS. var font = new Font(face, 24); var glyphs = new GlyphBuffer(); string text = "office"; TextShaper.ShapeRun(text, 0, text.Length, font, new RunProperties { Script = Script.Latin }, glyphs); for (int i = 0; i < glyphs.Count; i++) { ushort id = glyphs.GlyphIds[i]; int cluster = glyphs.Clusters[i]; // index in text the glyph came from GlyphPosition position = glyphs.Positions[i]; // in the font's units (pixels here) bool breakable = (glyphs.Flags[i] & GlyphFlags.UnsafeToBreak) == 0; } float width = glyphs.Advance; GlyphFlags.UnsafeToBreak marks where breaking the text needs shaping again; line layout uses it to re-shape only there. A run is one script in one direction; TextShaper.Shape splits real text into runs. The engine gives exactly hb-shape's glyphs, clusters, positions and flags on HarfBuzz's own tests and on Egami's corpus. Shaping text TextShaper.Shape shapes a whole string: it splits it into lines at hard breaks ( , , , U+0085, U+2028, U+2029), resolves each line's bidi levels, splits the line into runs of one level, one script, one span and one font, shapes each run as ShapeRun does and returns the runs in display order. Nothing wraps; that is line layout's job. // Whole text: lines at hard breaks, bidi levels, script runs, fallback fonts, runs in display order. var font = new Font(face, 24); var options = new ShapingOptions { Fallback = new FontFallback(fonts.Families) }; ShapedText shaped = TextShaper.Shape("Shalom: \u05E9\u05DC\u05D5\u05DD!", font, options); float x = 0; foreach (ShapedRun run in shaped.Lines[0].Runs) { GlyphRun glyphs = run.ToGlyphRun(new System.Numerics.Vector2(x, 0), shaped.Text); // what a canvas draws x += run.Advance; } ShapedText.Lines holds a ShapedLine per line, with its ParagraphLevel, its Runs from left to right, its Advance and the highest ascent and lowest descent of its fonts. Each ShapedRun has its Font, BidiLevel, Script, Language, text range and GlyphBuffer; ToGlyphRun turns it into the GlyphRun a canvas draws. ShapingOptions.Direction is Auto by default: each paragraph takes the direction of its first strong character. ShapingOptions.Spans give ranges their own font, language or features; spans must not overlap. // A styled range: its own font, language or features. var options = new ShapingOptions { Language = "en", Spans = [new TextSpan(6, 6) { Font = font with { Kerning = false }, Features = [FontFeature.SmallCaps] }], }; ShapedText shaped = TextShaper.Shape("Hello, World", font, options); Font fallback A font that does not map a character draws .notdef, unless ShapingOptions.Fallback names fonts to try. Fallback works on whole grapheme clusters, so a letter and its accents, or an emoji sequence, stay in one font: the first font that maps every character of the cluster takes it. The span's font comes first, then the FontFallback.Families (matched to the font's style), then the FontFallback.Resolver. Spaces and punctuation stay in the font before them when it has them, so fallback does not split words. Emoji presentation (a default-emoji character or VS16) prefers a color face (COLR, sbix or CBDT); VS15 prefers an outline face. // Characters the font lacks: the caller's families first, then installed fonts only when asked for. FontFallback mine = new(FontCollection.System.Families.Where(f => f.Name is "Segoe UI Emoji" or "Noto Color Emoji")); FontFallback system = FontFallback.System; // depends on the machine's fonts FontFallback none = FontFallback.None; // the default: missing characters draw as .notdef FontFallback.None, the default, keeps output independent of the machine: only the fonts passed are used. FontFallback.System resolves from the installed fonts through SystemFontFallback: fixed families per script on Windows, macOS and Linux (Segoe UI Emoji, Apple Color Emoji or Noto Color Emoji for emoji; the language picks Japanese, Chinese or Korean faces for Han), then any installed face that maps the cluster. Output then depends on the fonts installed. An IFontFallbackResolver of your own receives the cluster's text, script, language and the font's style. Features A FontFeature sets one OpenType feature for the whole run or a range of it: 0 turns a default feature off, 1 turns a feature on, higher values pick an alternate. FontFeature.Parse reads HarfBuzz's syntax (liga=0, +smcp, ss01, aalt=2, kern[3:5]=0); the presets cover common cases. // HarfBuzz's feature syntax, or the presets. FontFeature noLigatures = FontFeature.Parse("liga=0"); FontFeature figures = FontFeature.TabularFigures; FontFeature alternates = FontFeature.StylisticSet(1); FontFeature someKerning = FontFeature.Parse("kern[0:3]=0"); // off for the first three characters only var properties = new RunProperties { Features = [noLigatures, figures] }; TextShaper.ShapeRun(text, 0, text.Length, font, properties, glyphs); Layout tables Typeface.Layout returns an OpenTypeLayout, which lists the scripts, language systems and features the font's GSUB and GPOS offer. A table whose structure is damaged is ignored whole, with a Font.BadTable diagnostic, as HarfBuzz ignores it; a font that drives shaping past its limits stops with Font.ShapingLimit. // What the font's layout tables list. OpenTypeLayout layout = face.Layout; IReadOnlyList<FontTag> scripts = layout.Scripts; // DFLT, cyrl, grek, latn IReadOnlyList<FontTag> languages = layout.GetLanguageSystems(new FontTag("latn")); IReadOnlyList<FontTag> features = layout.GetFeatures(new FontTag("latn")); // liga, kern, ...

articles/guides/vp8.html.title: VP8 video frames | Egami
articles/guides/vp8.html.summary: VP8 video frames Vp8StreamDecoder decodes VP8 video (RFC 6386) a frame at a time: key frames and inter frames, motion vectors, the last, golden and alternate references and hidden frames. Every frame equals libvpx's sample for sample, on libvpx's own test vectors and on clips made with its encoder, across the four versions, one to eight token partitions, segmentation and odd sizes. It reads frames, not files: WebM and IVF are read by Egami.Video, which uses this decoder, and frames from any other source decode the same way. // VP8 frames in stream order, here from an IVF file (Egami.Video reads WebM and IVF for you). using Vp8StreamDecoder decoder = new() { ConcealErrors = false }; YuvRaster<byte>? picture = null; foreach (byte[] packet in IvfFrames("clip.ivf")) { Vp8FrameInfo info = decoder.Decode(packet); if (!info.IsShown) { continue; // a hidden frame, typically an alternate reference: it only updates the references } picture ??= YuvRaster.Create(info.Width, info.Height, ChromaFormat.Yuv420, YuvColor.Bt601Limited); decoder.CopyFrameTo(picture); // the picture is the caller's: change it or keep it shown++; } picture?.Dispose(); Decode takes the frames in stream order and returns a Vp8FrameInfo: whether the frame is a key frame and whether it is shown, the frame size from the last key frame, and the VP8 version. A hidden frame, typically an alternate reference, only updates the references and has no picture. CopyFrameTo copies a shown frame's planes into a 4:2:0 8-bit YuvRaster of the frame's size; the copy belongs to the caller, so it can be changed or kept while later frames decode. VP8 pictures are BT.601, limited range. Broken data Decoding starts at a key frame. By default a broken frame (data that runs out, a header that cannot be read) or an inter frame with no key frame before it throws CorruptDataException, and the decoder carries on from the next frame it is given; Reset drops the references so the next frame must be a key frame again. With ConcealErrors set nothing throws for broken data: the macroblocks a frame could not read are copied from the previous frame (mid-gray when there is none), a frame whose header cannot be read shows the previous frame again, and an inter frame with no key frame before it predicts from mid-gray. Vp8FrameInfo.IsConcealed says which frames were concealed. A key frame larger than the context's SafetyLimits throws LimitExceededException either way. Memory and threads The decoder keeps four frame buffers, which the references and the frame being decoded share as libvpx shares them, so a stream holds four frames however long it is. They come from the context's IPixelMemorySource and go back when the decoder is disposed. A frame's macroblock rows decode in a wavefront on up to EgamiContext.MaxParallelism threads, as many as the frame's token partitions allow (one partition decodes on one thread, as in libvpx); the result does not depend on the thread count. Decoding takes at most 1.5 times libvpx's time at 720p and 1080p, on one thread and on all cores.

articles/guides/webp.html.title: WebP | Egami
articles/guides/webp.html.summary: WebP Egami reads and writes WebP: lossless (VP8L), lossy (VP8) with or without alpha, and animated, written from RFC 9649 and RFC 6386 with no native code. WebpFormat.Info is registered in EgamiContext.Default, so Raster.Load recognizes WebP from its first bytes and Save("x.webp") picks the writer. Writing // Lossy, the default for rasters not read from WebP: quality 0 to 100 and effort 0 to 6 on cwebp's scales. photo.Save("small.webp", new WebpWriterOptions { Quality = 80 }); // Lossless: every pixel exact, colors under full transparency included. Effort 0 (fastest) to 6 (smallest). photo.Save("duck.webp", new WebpWriterOptions { Lossless = true, Effort = 6 }); // A raster read from a WebP file keeps its kind when saved with the defaults. using Raster again = Raster.Load("duck.webp"); again.Save("copy.webp"); WebpWriterOptions follows libwebp's own knobs, so the same numbers give about the same files as cwebp: Option Default Does Lossless null true writes VP8L, false VP8; null keeps the kind of the WebP file the raster came from (WebpDetails.Lossless) and writes lossy otherwise Quality 75 Lossy quality, 0 to 100, cwebp's -q scale Effort 4 0 (fastest) to 6 (smallest), cwebp's -m, for both kinds AlphaQuality 100 Lossy files with transparency: 100 keeps alpha exact KeepTransparentColors true Colors under fully transparent pixels are kept (exactly in lossless files); false lets the encoder change them for smaller files SharpYuv false Lossy: a slower color conversion that keeps sharp colored edges NearLossless 100 Lossless: below 100 pixel values may move a little before coding MixedFrames false Animations: each frame is encoded both ways and the smaller kept FirstFrameOnly false Writes only the first frame, as a still Lossy files with transparency carry the alpha in an ALPH chunk: compressed losslessly with the filter that gives the smallest result (all four tried at effort 5 and 6), and with fewer levels when AlphaQuality is below 100, fully transparent and fully opaque pixels always kept exact. Lossless WebP holds sides up to 16,384 pixels and lossy up to 16,383; larger rasters throw before any work. Every pixel type can be saved: it is converted to 8-bit RGBA first. Reading Raster.Load gives Rgba8 when the file says it has alpha (the VP8X flag, the VP8L hint or an ALPH chunk) and Rgb8 otherwise. Lossless files decode to exactly libwebp's pixels. Lossy files decode to libwebp's YUV planes sample for sample, and to RGB within one level of libwebp's: chroma is brought to full resolution exactly as libwebp's default upsampler does, then converted with the BT.601 kernel of the planar YUV guide. YuvRaster.Load returns a lossy file's planes untouched (4:2:0, BT.601, limited range, chroma in the centre), with the alpha as a fourth plane. Every kind streams through RasterDecoder, with regions, reductions and incremental decode. The same VP8 decoder reads video frames too, inter frames included: see VP8 video frames. WebpReaderOptions adds two choices on top of the general reader options: using Raster image = Raster.Load("duck.webp", options: new WebpReaderOptions { UseBackgroundColor = true, // animations: start from the ANIM background color instead of transparent FastUpsampling = true, // lossy files: repeat chroma samples instead of interpolating }); Format details and metadata ICC profiles, EXIF and XMP are read into RasterMetadata and written back unchanged. WebP has no resolution field, so the resolution is read from the EXIF block and written into it, in a minimal EXIF block when the raster has none. IPTC has no place in WebP and is not written. WebpDetails says what kind of file it was and keeps chunks Egami does not read, each a WebpChunk with its WebpChunkPosition; animation frames carry WebpFrameDetails. using Raster<Rgba8> image = Raster.Load<Rgba8>("duck.webp"); WebpDetails webp = (WebpDetails)image.Metadata.FormatDetails!; Console.WriteLine($"{(webp.Lossless ? "lossless" : "lossy")}, extended: {webp.Extended}, alpha: {webp.HasAlpha}"); // Chunks Egami does not read are kept and written back where they were. foreach (WebpChunk chunk in webp.OtherChunks) { Console.WriteLine($"{chunk.Type}: {chunk.Data.Length} bytes, {chunk.Position}"); } // An animation's frames say whether each was stored lossless. foreach (Frame<Rgba8> frame in image.Frames) { Console.WriteLine(frame.Metadata.FormatDetails is WebpFrameDetails { Lossless: true } ? "lossless frame" : "lossy frame"); } Animation Animated WebP reads and writes through the same frames as GIF and APNG. Reading composes every frame on a canvas exactly as libwebp's animation decoder does (its blending and key frames included), starting transparent unless WebpReaderOptions.UseBackgroundColor asks for the ANIM background color; ReaderOptions.Frames and streaming through RasterDecoder work as for GIF, holding one canvas whatever the frame count. Writing stores each frame's changed rectangle at even offsets, blended over the canvas when its new pixels are opaque and replacing them otherwise, with delays rounded to whole milliseconds and capped at 16,777,215. // A GIF (or APNG) becomes an animated WebP in one Load and one Save: frames, delays and loop count carry over. Each frame // stores only what changed; lossless frames are exact, MixedFrames keeps whichever kind is smaller per frame. using Raster gif = Raster.Load("pan.gif"); gif.Save("pan.webp", new WebpWriterOptions { Lossless = false, MixedFrames = true }); // Read back, every frame is the composed canvas, as with GIF and APNG. using Raster<Rgba8> webp = Raster.Load<Rgba8>("pan.webp"); foreach (Frame<Rgba8> frame in webp.Frames) { Console.WriteLine($"{frame.Metadata.Delay.TotalMilliseconds} ms, changed {frame.Metadata.Bounds}, blend {frame.Metadata.Blend}"); }

articles/packages.html.title: Packages | Egami
articles/packages.html.summary: Packages Egami is a family of packages. Each is fully managed C# with no dependencies outside the family, and you add only the ones you use. Packages at 1.0 or above keep their public API compatible within the major version; packages at 0.x may still change. Package Version What it does Needs Guides Egami 1.x Rasters and pixel types, every format reader and writer, operations, color management, metadata, streaming decode Nothing Getting started, Formats and most guides Egami.Drawing 1.0 Antialiased paths, shapes, strokes, clips, paints, layers, meshes and recorded drawings on a canvas Egami, Egami.Fonts Drawing, The .egdr format Egami.Fonts 1.0 TrueType and OpenType fonts, glyph outlines and metrics, subsetting, text shaping and paragraph layout Egami Fonts and text, Unicode text and shaping, Paragraph layout Egami.Svg 1.0 Reads SVG 1.1 and SVG 2 into an editable element tree, saves it back, and draws it onto any canvas Egami, Egami.Drawing, Egami.Fonts, Egami.Css SVG Egami.Css 1.0 CSS syntax, selectors, the cascade, media queries and value parsers Nothing CSS Egami.Metafiles 1.0 Plays WMF, EMF and EMF+ pictures onto a canvas Egami, Egami.Drawing, Egami.Fonts Windows metafiles The changelog lists what each version adds.

articles/performance.html.title: Performance | Egami
articles/performance.html.summary: Performance Tips that matter Load in the type you will work in. Raster.Load<Rgba8> converts row by row while decoding; loading the natural type and converting afterwards touches every pixel twice. Use Derive for thumbnails. It reads the source once and writes only the small result; Copy then Apply copies the full image first. Decode small. ReaderOptions.MinimumSize decodes JPEG at 1/2, 1/4 or 1/8 scale straight from the DCT, and averages blocks of rows as they are decoded for every other format, so a thumbnail never holds the full image. Stream large files. Raster.Transcode and RasterDecoder hold a few rows instead of the whole image; a leading crop or resize in a transcode chain becomes a decode region or reduction. Chain operations. A chain is planned as a whole: a Crop before a resize reads only the crop, adjacent color steps run as one pass, and AutoOrient before a resize turns only the result. Probe before you load when you might reject the file. Batch work on one thread per image (MaxParallelism = 1) and run images side by side; for a single large image, leave MaxParallelism at the processor count. Dispose rasters. Pixel memory is pooled; disposing returns it at once for the next image. Running the benchmarks dotnet run -c Release --project benchmarks/Egami.Benchmarks -- --filter "*" dotnet run -c Release --project benchmarks/Egami.Benchmarks -- --filter "*SimpleDecode*" The benchmarks use BenchmarkDotNet and generated test images (a 1920 × 1080 photo-like image and a screenshot-like one), so anyone can reproduce them. Egami's numbers Median times on one machine (24 cores, .NET 10, x64 with AVX2), decoding from memory into the file's natural pixel type: Scenario 1 thread All cores BMP 24-bit decode, 1920 × 1080 0.31 ms 0.37 ms BMP 8-bit palette decode 1.6 ms 1.7 ms TGA 32-bit RLE decode 3.1 ms 2.9 ms QOI decode, photo 15.3 ms 15.6 ms PPM decode 0.32 ms 0.39 ms QOI encode, photo 14.3 ms 14.4 ms TGA 32-bit RLE encode 3.6 ms 3.6 ms BMP 24-bit encode 0.46 ms 0.46 ms Steady-state decoding and encoding allocate only the result raster: under 2.5 KB of managed memory a call for these formats.

index.html.title: Egami | Egami
index.html.summary: Egami Egami is an open source 2D imaging library for .NET 10 that loads, edits, draws and saves images. MIT-licensed, with no strings for commercial use. Fully managed C#: no native binaries, no P/Invoke, and no third-party dependencies. Safe on untrusted files: sizes are checked before anything is allocated, and every reader is fuzz-tested. Trimming and Native AOT clean, on every OS and CPU .NET 10 supports. Formats: PNG and APNG, JPEG, GIF, WebP, BMP, TGA, QOI, the Netpbm formats, TIFF, Radiance and OpenEXR, JPEG XL, ICO and CUR read and written; AVIF, JPEG 2000, JBIG2, CCITT fax and PSD read. See Formats. Operations: resizing and geometry, color management, tone and color, filters, compositing, masks, analysis and palettes. More packages: vector drawing (Egami.Drawing), fonts and text layout (Egami.Fonts), SVG (Egami.Svg), CSS (Egami.Css) and Windows metafiles (Egami.Metafiles). See Packages. using Egami; using Raster image = Raster.Load("photo.jpg"); image.Apply(ops => ops.AutoOrient().Fit(800, 800)); image.Save("photo-small.png"); Start with Getting started, browse the guides and the cookbook, or look anything up in the API reference.
